Root causes (descriptive)

The logger measures the air temperature near the door or on the pallet surface. The product mass can stay within range because of thermal mass. A brief air temperature excursion can occur without a product temperature excursion. Common root causes include:

- The dock door opens and lets warm, humid air into the refrigerated space.
- The handoff time is longer than the validated time because of staff, paperwork, or equipment delays.
- The logger is placed near the door, on the outside of the load, or in dead air space.
- The dock seal, shelter, or air curtain is missing, broken, or not used.
- The refrigerated unit is off or in defrost during the handoff.
- The logger is out of calibration.
- The setpoint is too close to the upper limit. The temperature crosses 8°C during normal control swings.

These are common causes. The exact cause depends on your equipment, your procedure, and the logger model.

Corrective actions (procedural)

- Check the logger calibration certificate.
- If the certificate is expired or the accuracy is out of tolerance, replace the logger.
- Review the time and temperature data.
- Compare the logger time to the handoff record.
- Inspect the dock door seal and the air curtain.
- If they are defective, repair them.
- Retrain the staff on the handoff procedure.
- Confirm that the procedure specifies a maximum door-open time.
- Move the handoff point closer to the refrigerated storage.
- Alternatively, use an insulated transfer container.
- Adjust the truck or dock setpoint to provide margin.
- Do not set it below the product's lower limit.
- Change the logger placement.
- Put the logger inside the product load.
- Alternatively, put the logger in a validated location that represents product temperature.
- After each change, do a qualification or a mapping study to confirm that the process stays within the range.

Product disposition basis (descriptive)

This answer assumes that the product requires storage from 2°C to 8°C. The release decision depends on the product stability data, the regulatory requirements, and your quality system. No universal rule applies to all pharmaceutical products. The recorded air temperature is not the same as the product core temperature. Some products tolerate brief excursions above 8°C. Others do not. The manufacturer or the marketing authorization holder can give the product-specific excursion limit.

Product disposition triage (procedural)

- Quarantine the affected product.
- Do not release the product based only on the air temperature record.
- Until a qualified person completes the assessment, prevent release.
- Check the logger data against the product stability profile.
- Record these values:
  - Maximum temperature.
  - Duration above 8°C.
  - Time above the excursion limit.
- If the product stability data include a mean kinetic temperature limit, calculate that value.
- If the product-specific excursion limit is not available, hold the product in quarantine until you get that data.
- Contact the manufacturer or the marketing authorization holder.
- Request a written stability assessment for the recorded excursion.
- Document these items:
  - The evidence.
  - The assessment.
  - The disposition decision.
- If the product is released, keep the excursion record with the batch file.
- If the product is rejected, follow your procedure for destruction or return.

## Nested-data support

`application/json` represents nested objects and arrays as first-class structures. `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and `multipart/form-data` carry flat name-value pairs. Some clients express nested data with bracket keys such as `user[address][city]`. This convention is not part of the media type. Server frameworks differ in whether they convert these keys back into nested structures.

RFC 8259 does not reject duplicate object keys. Parser behavior for duplicate keys varies by implementation. Many parsers convert JSON numbers to 64-bit floating point values, so large integers can lose precision. Some JSON parsers set a maximum nesting depth. A payload beyond that limit causes an error. JSON object key order is not significant, although some parsers preserve insertion order.

## Binary payloads

`application/json` is a text format. Raw binary bytes must be converted to text, usually with base64. Base64 adds about 33 percent overhead. Large binary values increase memory and CPU use when a client encodes or decodes them.

`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is not suitable for raw binary. A byte outside the unreserved set becomes three characters, which can triple the payload size.

`multipart/form-data` can carry raw binary in separate parts. Each part can include a `Content-Disposition` header with a filename. Each part can include its own `Content-Type` header. For `multipart/form-data`, the Content-Type header must include the boundary parameter. The boundary string must not appear in any part, or the parse result is invalid. A client normally chooses a random boundary to prevent collisions.

## Server parse load

`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` has a simple parse process. The server splits the body on ampersand characters, then splits each pair on the first equals character. The CPU cost is low. Many server implementations read the full body into memory. The standard allows duplicate field names and empty values, but framework behavior varies. The format requires that a client send a literal plus sign as `%2B` because `+` means a space.

`application/json` requires a full parse to an object graph before the server can act. A JSON parser must handle escape sequences, UTF-8, and number syntax. The parse cost grows with payload size and nested depth. Most JSON parsers do not stream partial results. Some parsers set a depth limit to prevent stack overflow. A server often sets a size limit for JSON bodies.

`multipart/form-data` often has the highest server load of the three. The server scans for boundary markers and parses headers for each part. Large parts can spill to temporary files on disk. Many small parts increase overhead because each part needs separate headers. Frameworks that buffer all parts in memory can exhaust memory with large uploads. Servers often enforce size and part-count limits to prevent denial of service.

The return statement in a finally block takes precedence over a return statement in the try block. The Java runtime evaluates the try block's return value first. Then it executes the finally block before the method returns. A return statement in the finally block replaces the value from the try block.

If the try block throws an exception and the finally block completes normally, the exception propagates to the caller after the finally block finishes. The normal completion of the finally block does not suppress the exception. If the finally block has a return statement instead, that return statement suppresses the exception.

Default-deny inbound policy blocks all traffic that an explicit rule does not allow. A permissive policy only blocks traffic that matches known-bad indicators.

For incident response, default-deny creates a small set of permitted paths. Logs contain only expected traffic and rejected attempts. Analysts can identify unusual activity faster because deviations stand out. False positives occur when a missing rule blocks legitimate business traffic. These false positives consume incident response time.

A permissive policy permits most traffic and logs more events. Legitimate traffic mixes with suspicious traffic. Analysts must inspect more data to find threats. Known-bad lists do not stop new or unknown attacks. Therefore, a permissive policy can let a novel attack enter without any alert.

For operational overhead, default-deny requires an inventory of every required business flow. It requires you to update rules before you add a new server or service. Cloud SaaS providers often use dynamic IP addresses. This makes allow rules for inbound callbacks difficult to maintain. Missed rules cause outages and urgent change requests.

A permissive policy requires less initial rule design. It replaces that work with maintenance of blocklists and threat intelligence feeds. Those feeds require regular updates and false positive review. Over time you can accumulate many exception rules. That reduces the clarity of the policy.

In summary, default-deny reduces attack surface and improves incident detection but increases rule maintenance. Permissive reduces immediate operational friction but increases log volume and unknown threat exposure. For a mid-sized company with hybrid infrastructure, default-deny inbound is usually a safer baseline for on-premises servers. A separate policy can handle cloud SaaS services that require outbound controls or provider-specific inbound allowances. The correct choice depends on your tolerance for downtime and your security staffing.

Before you start the spindle, complete these checks:

- Wear safety glasses. Do not wear gloves.
- Remove loose clothing and jewelry. Tie back long hair.
- Remove all loose items from the machine table.
- Check that the cutter is sharp, clean, and free of damage.
- Check that the cutter is tight in the spindle.
- Check that the drawbar is tight.
- Check that the machine guard is in place.
- Check that the spindle direction is clockwise from above.
- Check that all table locks are free.
- Check that the emergency stop button works.
- Check that the vise is tight on the table.
- Check that the work area is dry.

Secure the workpiece:

1. Clean the vise base, the jaws, and the table.
2. Put two clean parallels on the vise base.
3. Put the block on the parallels.
4. Tighten the vise handle. Do not use a hammer on the handle.
5. Tap the top of the block with a soft dead-blow hammer.
6. Try to move the parallels by hand. They must not move.
7. Try to move the block by hand. It must not move.
8. Check that the top of the block is above the vise jaws. The cutter must not hit the jaws.

Select the cutter:

- Use a sharp face mill or fly cutter for aluminum.
- A fly cutter with one sharp high-speed steel tool bit also works for light cuts.
- Choose a cutter with a diameter that is larger than the block width.
- For a small block, a 2-inch to 3-inch diameter face mill is common.
- Use a cutter with positive rake and polished flutes for aluminum.
- Do not use a worn or dull cutter.

Set speed and feed:

Decide if the cutter is high-speed steel (HSS) or carbide.

- For HSS, use a cutting speed of 300 SFM.
- For carbide, use a cutting speed of 500 SFM.

Calculate the spindle speed with this formula:
`RPM = (12 * CS) / (π * D)`

- CS is the cutting speed in surface feet per minute.
- D is the cutter diameter in inches.

For a 2-inch HSS cutter, CS = 300, D = 2. The result is about 573 RPM. Use 500 RPM on the machine.

For a 2-inch carbide cutter, CS = 500, D = 2. The result is about 955 RPM. Use 950 RPM on the machine.

Set the feed per tooth:

- For HSS, use 0.002 inch per tooth.
- For carbide, use 0.003 inch per tooth.

Calculate the feed rate with this formula:
`Feed rate = RPM * number of teeth * feed per tooth`

For a 4-tooth HSS cutter at 500 RPM, the feed rate is 500 * 4 * 0.002 = 4 IPM. Use 3 IPM on the machine.

For a 4-tooth carbide cutter at 950 RPM, the feed rate is 950 * 4 * 0.003 = 11.4 IPM. Use 10 IPM on the machine.

If you feed by hand, move the table slowly and steadily. Do not force the feed.

Set the depth of cut to 0.010 inch for the first pass.

Face the block:

1. Move the table so the cutter is clear of the block.
2. Lower the quill or raise the knee until the cutter lightly touches the paper on the block.
3. Set the quill or knee dial to zero.
4. Move the table away from the block.
5. Raise the knee or lower the quill by 0.010 inch.
6. Lock the knee or quill after you set the depth.
7. Start the spindle. Wait until the spindle reaches full speed.
8. Engage the power feed or turn the hand wheel at a steady rate.
9. Feed the table across the whole block until the cut is complete.
10. Stop the spindle. Wait for the cutter to stop.
11. Check the surface finish and flatness.
12. If more material must be removed, repeat these steps with another 0.010 inch cut.

If the cutter is narrower than the block width, take multiple passes. Overlap each pass by half the cutter diameter.

Safety during the cut:

- If the machine vibrates or makes a loud noise, stop the spindle immediately.
- Do not leave the machine unattended while it is on.
- Keep your hands away from the cutter when the spindle is on.
- If the workpiece moves during the cut, stop the spindle immediately.
- Do not try to hold the workpiece by hand.

After the cut:

- Clean chips with a brush. Do not use compressed air.
- Loosen the vise and remove the block. The edges can be sharp.
- Deburr sharp edges with a file.

For a containerized application suite, three approaches store and rotate database credentials and API keys:

- Environment variables
- A dedicated secret manager such as HashiCorp Vault
- Encrypted configuration files

The recommended approach depends on the deployment size and the threat model.

Environment variables are simple to use. Operators can set them in the container image or in the orchestration manifest. They do not require a network call at startup. However, many container runtimes expose environment variables through the process table and the orchestration API. Rotation requires a change to the manifest and a rolling restart of the affected containers. This approach gives low security for secrets because the values remain visible in several places.

A dedicated secret manager such as HashiCorp Vault stores secrets in a central location. Applications request secrets at runtime through the Vault API. The manager can issue short-lived credentials for databases and cloud APIs. It can also rotate those credentials automatically. Operators must secure the authentication token that applications use to reach Vault.

This approach requires extra infrastructure and configuration. The security is higher because secrets do not live in environment variables or files. Vault can restrict access per application and provide an audit log. Rotation can occur without a container restart when the application requests a new secret.

Encrypted configuration files store secrets in a file that is encrypted at rest. Operators decrypt the file when the container starts. Tools such as SOPS or age provide encryption. This approach is simple for small deployments. Rotation requires a new encrypted file and a container restart.

The main risk is the decryption key. If the key is stored with the file, the encryption gives little protection. The key must live in a separate secure location, such as a key management service.

For production, a dedicated secret manager is the recommended approach. It provides strong security and automated rotation. Environment variables are suitable only for non-secret configuration values. Encrypted configuration files are suitable for small deployments where a secret manager is not practical. The threat model determines the best choice. No single approach suits every containerized suite.

Optimization finds the best value of a function subject to constraints.

Objective function

A candidate solution is a possible input to the objective function. The objective function is the quantity that the problem must minimize or maximize. It maps each candidate solution to a numeric value. The problem statement identifies this function before the search begins. A lower value is better for a minimization problem. A higher value is better for a maximization problem.

Feasible region

The feasible region is the set of all points that satisfy every constraint. Constraints can be equations or inequalities. Solutions outside this region do not obey the problem rules. The search occurs only inside this region. If the feasible region is empty, the problem has no solution.

Local optimum

A solution is a local optimum if no nearby feasible solution has a more favorable objective value. The word nearby depends on the distance measure for the problem. A problem can have many local optima. A local optimum can exist far from the global optimum.

Global optimum

A global optimum is a feasible solution that has the most favorable objective value over the entire feasible region. A global optimum is also a local optimum. A problem can have more than one global optimum if multiple feasible solutions have the same best value. Not every local optimum is a global optimum.

Use the same Python version and operating system for lock creation and installation.

1. Create and activate a virtual environment.
2. Install pip-tools in this environment.
   ```
   python -m pip install pip-tools
   ```
3. Write direct dependencies in a file named requirements.in.
   Write one line for each direct dependency.
   To pin a direct dependency, use an exact version.
   For example:
   ```
   requests[security]==2.31.0
   ```
   If you need ranges, pip-compile resolves them to exact versions.
4. If an existing requirements.txt lock file exists, copy it to requirements.txt.bak.
5. Generate the lock file with hashes.
   ```
   pip-compile --generate-hashes requirements.in -o requirements.txt
   ```
6. Examine requirements.txt.
   Confirm that each package line has an exact version with `==`.
   Confirm that the file has no unpinned packages.
7. Commit requirements.txt to version control.
8. Install dependencies only from the lock file.
   ```
   pip-sync requirements.txt
   ```

Handle package extras:

- Put each extra on the direct dependency line in requirements.in.
- After you compile, find the package line in requirements.txt.
- Confirm that the extra remains in that line.
- If you use pyproject.toml for optional dependencies, compile each extras group separately.
  Use this command:
  ```
  pip-compile pyproject.toml --extra test -o requirements-test.txt
  ```
  Generate one lock file for each extra group.

Handle build dependencies:

- Keep build dependencies in the `[build-system]` section of pyproject.toml.
- Pin each build dependency to an exact version in that section.
- pip-tools does not lock build dependencies from pyproject.toml automatically.
- To lock build dependencies, create a file named requirements-build.in.
- Add pip, setuptools, and wheel to requirements-build.in with exact versions.
- Compile the build lock file with unsafe packages allowed.
  ```
  pip-compile --allow-unsafe requirements-build.in -o requirements-build.txt
  ```
- Install build dependencies from that build lock file before you build packages without isolation.

If pip-compile fails, restore requirements.txt.bak.
If pip-sync fails, reinstall from the last known good lock file.

Blame tracking inserts runtime checks at boundaries between typed and untyped code. Each boundary cast carries two blame labels: one for the typed side and one for the untyped side. When a check fails, the runtime assigns blame to the side that caused the failure. Typed code cannot be blamed for a failed check. This property is the blame theorem. It ensures soundness because all type errors from dynamic values are attributed to untyped code.

Higher-order functions create the main edge cases. A function cast is not checked immediately. It creates a wrapper function that checks each argument when the function is called. The wrapper also checks the result before it returns. Blame for an argument failure goes to the caller. Blame for a result failure goes to the function.

This split is required because function types are contravariant in their argument type. Therefore blame can reverse direction when a function value crosses a boundary. A function that returns another function needs a recursive wrapper. Each nested function gets its own checks and blame labels.

Functions that cross the same boundary multiple times can accumulate wrappers. Each wrapper preserves the original blame labels, so the first failure still identifies the correct side. These rules preserve the blame theorem for higher-order code.

Use this procedure for a CCS2 DC fast charge at a depot.

Complete these prerequisites before you connect.
1. Review the site emergency procedures before you start.
2. Park the truck on a level surface.
3. Set the parking brake.
4. Turn the vehicle ignition off.
5. Check that the charger is idle and shows no fault.
6. Check that the charge area is dry and clear of ice.
7. Check that your hands are dry.
8. Stand on a dry surface.
9. Wear the personal protective equipment that your site requires.

Inspect the charge cable and the CCS2 connector before each use.
1. Inspect the full cable length.
2. Look for cuts, cracks, burns, bulges, or exposed conductors.
3. Inspect the connector housing for cracks or deformation.
4. Check the connector pins for bends, corrosion, dirt, or moisture.
5. Do not touch the connector pins.
6. Check the locking latch and the strain relief at both ends.
7. Keep the cable away from the truck wheels.
8. If you find damage, do not use this charger.
9. A damaged cable can cause electric shock.
10. Tag the charger as unserviceable.
11. Report the damaged charger.

Perform these cold weather checks before you connect.
1. Check the battery temperature on the vehicle display.
2. If the battery temperature is below the manufacturer minimum, activate the battery precondition operation from the vehicle controls.
3. Wait until the display shows that the precondition operation is complete.
4. Check that the battery temperature is in the normal charge range.
5. When the battery temperature is below the manufacturer limit, do not start a DC fast charge.
6. A cold charge can damage the battery.
7. If the precondition operation does not complete, report the fault.

Connect the connector to the truck.
1. If the charge port door is frozen, use the vehicle defrost function.
2. Open the vehicle charge port door.
3. Inspect the vehicle inlet for dirt, moisture, or damage.
4. Remove the CCS2 connector from the holster.
5. Align the connector with the vehicle inlet.
6. Push the connector fully into the inlet.
7. Check that the locking mechanism engages.
8. If the locking mechanism does not engage, do not start the session.
9. If the locking mechanism does not engage, remove the connector.
10. If the locking mechanism does not engage, check the connector for damage.
11. Check that the charger and the vehicle establish communication.
12. If communication does not establish, do not force the session.
13. If communication does not establish, remove the connector.
14. If communication does not establish, check the inlet.
15. If the charger does not start automatically, start the session from the charger display or the vehicle app.
16. Check that the charge current starts on the display.
17. Stay near the charger for the first minute.
18. Check for unusual heat, noise, or smell.
19. If you find unusual heat, noise, or smell, stop the session.

Stop and disconnect safely.
1. Stop the session from the charger display or the vehicle app.
2. Wait until the display shows zero current.
3. Check that the session is stopped.
4. While current flows, do not disconnect the connector.
5. An electric arc can cause injury.
6. Press the release latch.
7. Pull the connector straight out.
8. Do not force the connector.
9. Stow the cable in the holster without kinks.
10. Close the vehicle charge port door.
11. Inspect the cable and connector for new damage after each use.
12. If you find new damage, tag the charger.
13. If you find new damage, report it.

Emergency stop.
If you see smoke, sparks, or heat during the charge, press the emergency stop on the charger.
After the charger shows that the system is safe, disconnect the connector.

Use this procedure only as a general guide.
Follow the instructions from the truck and charger manufacturers.

Cursor-based pagination returns a page and a cursor. The cursor is an opaque string. The client must not parse the cursor. The client sends the cursor back to the server to request the next page.

For stable ordering, the server uses a sort key with unique values. If the sort key does not have unique values, the server adds a tiebreaker column. The first page returns items in ascending order by this sort key. The server encodes the sort key value of the last item into the cursor. For the next page, the server queries for items with sort key values greater than the cursor value. If the sort key is not unique, the cursor contains the tiebreaker value. The next query compares the composite key as follows: sort_key greater than cursor_sort_key OR sort_key equal to cursor_sort_key AND tiebreaker greater than cursor_tiebreaker. This condition ensures each item appears exactly once.

Insertions and deletions between pages have these effects:

- If a new item has a sort key value greater than the cursor value, later pages include that item.
- If a new item has a sort key value less than or equal to the cursor value, later pages do not include that item.
- If an item is deleted before the client requests the next page, later pages do not include that item.
- If an item is deleted after the client receives it, later pages are not affected.

To choose a good cursor field, follow these rules:

- The field must be unique. The field value identifies one item only.
- The field must be immutable. The field value does not change after the item is created.
- Prefer a monotonic field. New items have values greater than existing values.
- Prefer a field with high cardinality. Many distinct values reduce the chance of duplicate sort keys.

A common cursor field is a composite of a creation timestamp and a unique identifier.

A shift handoff transfers responsibility for ongoing work from outgoing personnel to incoming personnel. The essential elements are:

- current status
- completed work
- outstanding work
- safety issues
- abnormal conditions
- required actions

The exact elements vary by organization and by setting. For example, aviation maintenance uses an aircraft status log and a written turnover record. Hospital nursing uses a patient report that includes:

- diagnosis
- current condition
- treatment plan

The incoming person must repeat the key information to confirm understanding.

A structured format reduces loss of critical context because it follows a fixed sequence. The sequence covers all important elements. It does not rely on memory. Many nursing units use SBAR. SBAR stands for:

- Situation
- Background
- Assessment
- Recommendation

Aviation maintenance organizations use a written shift turnover log with headings. The outgoing person completes each heading before the shift ends.

The incoming person reads the log. The incoming person asks specific questions about unresolved items. This confirmation step catches missing information. Structured formats also provide a written record for later review. The record supports a safe transfer of responsibility. Use of these formats reduces the risk of loss of important details. No format can guarantee that all information transfers without error.

No, uniform slack per route does not always improve on-time performance. The effect depends on the network structure and the interaction between routes. Slack on every route can absorb local delays in some networks. In other networks, this slack can cause cascading delays. For example, a delayed vehicle can miss a connection with another vehicle if the planner places slack only at the end of the route. More effective strategies often place slack at critical transfer points or at routes that feed many other routes.

Root causes

Huge pull requests occur when a feature branch contains many unrelated changes. The team does not split the work into small tasks. A large request makes review slow and incomplete.

Vague comments occur when reviewers do not use a checklist or clear criteria. The reviewer writes 'fix this' and gives no file. The reviewer gives no line. The reviewer gives no reason. The author cannot act on that comment.

Authors do not respond well when the team has no response rules. The team must define how to reply. The team must define when to change code. The team must define when to ask questions. Without these rules, the discussion stops or becomes an argument.

These problems connect. A large request makes reviewers tired. Tired reviewers write vague comments. Authors then do not know how to respond.

Workflow steps

1. Split each task into small changes. Make each change address one problem only.
2. Keep each pull request small. Split a request that changes many files or functions.
3. Use a review checklist. Put the checklist in the pull request template.
4. Write each comment with these parts:
   - Location
   - Problem
   - Required action
5. Use these severity labels:
   - 'must fix' for defects
   - 'suggest' for optional changes
   - 'question' for clarifications
6. Define author response rules. Require the author to reply or change the code for each comment.
7. Set a review time limit. Agree on the limit and follow it.
8. If a request has unresolved 'must fix' comments, do not merge it.
9. If a discussion becomes long, move it to a call or chat. Post the decision in the pull request.
10. Hold a short retrospective regularly. Discuss what worked and what did not.

Synchronous all-reduce method: Each worker computes gradients on a local mini-batch. The workers use an all-reduce collective to average gradients across all workers. The model parameters update with the averaged gradient. All workers use the same parameter version before each step. Thus gradient staleness is zero. The method waits for the slowest worker at each step, and this wait can reduce hardware utilization.

Asynchronous parameter-server method: Workers pull parameters from a central or sharded parameter server. Each worker computes a gradient and pushes it to the server. The server applies each gradient immediately. A worker can pull a parameter version that does not include some recent gradients from other workers. The gradient staleness can be large. Staleness can harm convergence or cause divergence if the step size is large, but bounded staleness techniques limit this risk.

Convergence speed: Synchronous all-reduce often gives stable convergence per update. It can require a larger step size when the batch size grows. Asynchronous parameter server can show faster wall-clock progress because workers do not wait. It can need more steps to reach the same accuracy because stale gradients add noise. The actual choice depends on model type, cluster homogeneity, and network speed.

Scalability trade-offs: All-reduce scales well on homogeneous nodes with high-bandwidth low-latency interconnects. Communication time increases with model size and worker count. Parameter server can scale to many workers if the server is sharded. The server can become a bottleneck for large models. In practice, synchronous all-reduce is common for dense models on GPU clusters. Asynchronous parameter server is common for sparse models and heterogeneous workers.

Use this procedure to choose between microservices and a modular monolith.

0. Record the system requirements and constraints.
1. Assess team size.
   a. Record the number of engineers who build and operate the system.
   b. Record the number of teams that own parts of the system.
   c. Define a threshold for team size based on your context.
   d. If the team size is below the threshold, record the modular monolith as the recommendation for this area.
   e. If the team size is at or above the threshold, record microservices as the recommendation for this area.
2. Assess deployment needs.
   a. List the parts that must deploy independently.
   b. List the parts that can deploy together.
   c. If frequent independent deployments are required, record microservices as the recommendation for this area.
   d. If independent deployments are not required, record the modular monolith as the recommendation for this area.
3. Assess data boundaries.
   a. Identify business capabilities that own separate data.
   b. Identify shared data that spans business capabilities.
   c. If each capability owns its data, record microservices as the recommendation for this area.
   d. If data is shared across capabilities, record the modular monolith as the recommendation for this area.
4. Assess operational overhead.
   a. Estimate the cost to run many services.
   b. Estimate the cost to run one deployable unit.
   c. Compare the two cost estimates.
   d. If the cost of many services is acceptable, record microservices as the recommendation for this area.
   e. If the cost is not acceptable, record the modular monolith as the recommendation for this area.
5. Combine the findings.
   a. Record the recommendation from each area.
   b. Compare the recommendations.
   c. If the recommendations conflict, assign higher weight to operational overhead and data boundaries.
   d. Select the option with fewer conflicts.
6. Document the decision.
   a. Write the selected architecture.
   b. Write the evaluated criteria and results.
   c. Write the risks and trade-offs.
   d. Write the decision date and reviewers.
   e. Store the document in the team repository.

The system uses a common layered architecture. Each layer has one responsibility. The layers are:
- Presentation
- Business logic
- Data access

This structure separates concerns. It makes the system easier to maintain. This pattern is a common practice, not a formal guarantee.

The presentation layer receives input from users. It sends that input to the business logic layer. It shows results to users. It must not contain business rules. It must not access the data store directly.

The business logic layer contains the core rules. It validates data. It coordinates the work between the presentation layer and the data access layer. It does not know the details of the user interface or the database.

The data access layer reads data from a storage system. It writes data to that system. It makes the storage details available only as a simple interface to the business logic layer. This layer also translates storage errors into a form that the business logic can use.

Dependencies must point downward. A higher layer can depend on a lower layer. A lower layer must not depend on a higher layer. For example, the presentation layer can call the business logic layer. The business logic layer must not call the presentation layer. Every layer communicates through interfaces, not concrete classes.

Teams can deviate from strict layering for performance. Some queries join many tables. A strict path through three layers adds overhead. In that case, the presentation layer can call a dedicated data access method. This direct call bypasses the business logic layer. If the team bypasses a layer, the team must document the bypass. The team must write integration tests for the bypass.

Cross-layer concerns include:
- Audit logs
- Authentication
- Cache storage

These concerns apply to many layers. A strict layer does not own them cleanly. The system can use these components:
- Middleware
- Filters
- Interceptors

These components sit outside the normal layer path. The business logic layer and the data access layer must not duplicate that logic.

Third normal form (3NF) permits a non-prime attribute to depend on a non-superkey determinant. Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) requires every determinant to be a superkey. BCNF is strictly stronger than 3NF. These statements apply to functional dependencies only. Multivalued dependencies require fourth normal form.

BCNF removes all redundancy that follows from functional dependencies. 3NF can keep redundancy when a prime attribute depends on a non-superkey determinant. That redundancy can cause update anomalies.

For example, relation R(A, B, C) has candidate keys AB and AC and functional dependency C to B. This relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF. The C to B dependency permits duplicate B values for one C value. An update to one row must also update the other rows. A missed update creates an inconsistency.

BCNF can require more tables. Extra tables add join cost and application complexity. The extra decomposition is justified when writes are frequent and update anomalies can cause serious errors. It is also justified when the database must enforce integrity without application-level repair.

A dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition does not always exist. Some functional dependencies must then be enforced with triggers or application code. 3NF always permits a dependency-preserving, lossless decomposition. A table can stay in 3NF when the dependency that violates BCNF must be enforced inside that table.

Systems with many reads often use denormalization. Denormalization adds redundancy and can create update anomalies. The application or an ETL process must then manage the redundant data. Denormalization is justified when reads dominate and anomalies are rare or easy to repair.

Evolutionary architecture treats change as a normal part of a system's life. An architecture fitness function is an automated test that grades one quality attribute of a system. The term comes from genetic algorithms. In that field, a fitness function scores each candidate solution. Evolutionary architecture borrows this idea. It uses fitness functions to score architectural choices during change.

Fitness functions provide these benefits:
- They turn architectural rules into tests that run with the normal test suite.
- They give fast feedback when a change breaks a rule.
- They keep quality attributes visible during long-term development.

Architects define fitness functions for quality attributes such as performance, security, or maintainability. Teams can run fitness functions in a continuous integration pipeline. Fitness functions can act as mandatory or advisory gates. A mandatory function must pass before deployment. An advisory function reports a trend for review.

A simple fitness function can test response time. The function defines that 95 percent of requests to a service must complete within 500 milliseconds. The function runs a load test and compares the measured percentile to the limit. The function fails when the measured percentile exceeds the limit. This example is illustrative.

Key rotation improves security.
It adds operational work.
The main trade-off is security against availability and operational effort.

Rotation frequency:
These items set the correct frequency:
- The token lifetime.
- The sensitivity of the protected data.
- The level of automation.

Short rotation intervals reduce the time that a compromised key can sign forged tokens.
Each rotation requires coordination between the signer and every verifier.
Frequent rotation without automation causes mistakes and outages.
Systems with short-lived access tokens can rotate more often than systems with long-lived refresh tokens.
Key retirement must account for the longest token lifetime that the old key ever signed.

Overlap period:
An overlap period lets the old key verify tokens that the signer issued before the switch.
The overlap must be longer than the maximum lifetime for accepted tokens.
Add the maximum expected clock skew to this lifetime.
If the overlap is shorter, valid tokens can fail verification.
A longer overlap increases the time that a leaked old key can still verify tokens.
During the overlap, the signer must use the new key only.
The old key must stay active for verification only.
When no token that the old key signed remains unexpired, remove the old key.

Verification during transition:
Before the signer uses the new private key, it must publish the new public key to all verifiers.
A token must include a key identifier.
This identifier tells the verifier which key to use.
Verifiers must accept tokens signed with either key during the overlap.
If a verifier receives a token with an unknown key identifier, it must refresh its key set.
After the refresh, it must try to verify the token again.
The key set cache must have a time-to-live.
When the cache sees an unknown key identifier, it must refetch.
If a key is compromised, remove it from the active set.
Reject tokens that use that key.

Other trade-offs:
A key that rotates too rarely gives an attacker a long window after a leak.
A key that rotates too often without automation causes failed verifications.
This also increases re-authentication load.
The interval and the overlap must balance the risk window against the recovery ability of the system.
Test the rotation process in a staging environment.
This reduces the risk of production failures.
Exact intervals depend on the token format.
They also depend on the implementation and the deployment.

The client generates a unique key for each logical operation. An idempotency key is a client-generated value that identifies a request. The server creates a record for the key before it executes the request. The server stores the response with this record after processing.

Keys must have a scope. The scope can be one of these values:

- The client ID
- The user ID
- The resource ID

Key uniqueness must hold only within that scope. The server must store the scope with the record.

To handle concurrent requests with the same key, the server must enforce a unique constraint on the scope and the key. The record has these states:

- Incomplete
- Complete
- Failed

A second request that sees an incomplete record must wait or read the current state. A retry after a failed record can execute the request again.

Expiration must match the maximum allowed retry window. After the expiration time, the server can delete the record. Deletion after expiration is safe only if the client accepts a duplicate execution risk.

A retry with the same key after a complete response must return the stored response. If the client retries because of a network failure, the server must prevent a second execution. The server must store the response before it sends the response to the client. If the server crashes after execution but before storage, a retry can execute the request twice.

A request can have an external effect, for example a payment charge. The server must store the key before the external effect. If the external system does not return a response, the server does not know the outcome. In that case, the server must keep the record incomplete or set a state that requires manual resolution. The client can retry with a new key only when the server has proof that the previous attempt failed.

PREREQUISITES

Make sure that these items exist:
- Webhook event documentation with payload schema.
- A secrets manager for signature secrets.
- A durable store for processed identifiers.

PROCEDURE

1. Define the webhook events and payload schema.
2. Choose a signature algorithm. HMAC-SHA256 is common.
3. Generate a unique secret for each sender.
4. Store the secret in the secrets manager.
5. Configure the sender to include a signature header.
6. Configure the receiver to read the raw request body.
7. Compute the signature on the raw body with the shared secret.
8. Compare the computed signature with the received signature. Use a constant-time comparison.
9. If the signatures do not match, reject the request with status 401.
10. Record the event identifier from the header or the payload.
11. Check the identifier against stored processed identifiers.
12. If the identifier exists, return status 200.
13. If the identifier exists, do not process the event.
14. If the identifier does not exist, process the event.
15. After the event succeeds, store the identifier.
16. After the event succeeds, return status 200.
17. If the event fails, return a non-2xx status to request retry.
18. Use exponential backoff for retries.
19. Start with a delay.
20. Double the delay after each retry.
21. Add jitter to the delay.
22. Set a maximum retry count.
23. If retries exceed the maximum, log the failure.

WARNING

Do not process the same event more than once. Duplicate events can cause incorrect data.

TRADE-OFFS

Symmetric signatures use one shared secret. The receiver and the sender must protect the secret. Asymmetric signatures use a private key to sign and a public key to verify. The receiver stores only the public key. Asymmetric signatures require more computation than HMAC.

An exact-once delivery guarantee is not possible across an unreliable network. At-least-once delivery requires the receiver to deduplicate events. Identifiers must be stored in a database with a unique constraint. The identifier check and the insert must be atomic. A transaction or a conditional insert provides atomicity.

Immediate retries can overload a failing receiver. Exponential backoff reduces load but increases delivery delay. Jitter prevents synchronized retry storms from many senders. A maximum retry count prevents infinite retry loops. After the maximum retry count, the event typically goes to a dead-letter queue for manual review.

Zero trust architecture and perimeter-based security differ in their default trust model. Perimeter-based security trusts traffic inside the network boundary. It checks identity and device status mainly at the point of entry. Zero trust removes that default trust. It verifies each access request per session and per resource. This comparison describes common practice, not a formal guarantee. Implementations vary by product and environment.

Identity
Perimeter-based security treats network location as the primary identity signal. A user who reaches the internal network often receives broad access. Zero trust treats identity as a main signal. It also uses device posture and context. It requires continuous verification. It requires least privilege per session. It often requires multifactor authentication and device compliance. Credential theft has a larger effect in zero trust. The identity provider is a critical dependency.

Network microsegmentation
Perimeter-based security uses coarse segments such as VLANs and firewall zones. Traffic between hosts inside the same segment is usually allowed. Zero trust uses per-workload microsegmentation. It also uses per-resource microsegmentation. The default policy denies all traffic. Access rules use identity attributes. They also use resource attributes. They do not use only IP addresses. This approach reduces the attack surface of east-west traffic.

Lateral movement
In perimeter-based security, an attacker who enters the perimeter can often move between internal hosts. Flat networks and broad trust make lateral movement easier. Zero trust limits lateral movement with default deny. It also uses per-resource policies. It inspects internal traffic. It enforces least privilege. Zero trust does not eliminate lateral movement. Overbroad roles can still permit it. Stolen credentials can still permit it. Policy gaps can still permit it.

Edge cases and operational overhead
Zero trust can introduce operational costs that are often overlooked.
- Brownfield migration is difficult. Legacy applications can use hardcoded IP addresses. They can use service accounts. They can use shared administrator accounts. A migration requires an inventory of these dependencies before network policy changes.
- Policy management can become complex. Many fine-grained rules create a large policy surface. Stale rules can block legitimate work. A wrong policy can stop access with no clear error.
- The availability of the identity provider is an operational risk. If the identity provider fails, users cannot authenticate. The organization needs a tested break-glass procedure. The organization needs an audit trail for emergency access.
- Unmanaged devices often do not support zero trust agents. Operational technology often does not support zero trust agents. Printers can fail posture checks. Medical devices can fail posture checks. Industrial controllers can fail posture checks. An exception path is required for these devices.
- Policy enforcement points can create new failure modes. Traffic that must pass through a gateway can cause asymmetric routing. The same traffic can cause higher latency.
- Telemetry volume increases. Alert tuning is necessary to avoid missed incidents.
- Hybrid environments often have multiple policy engines. Consistent policy across on-premises and cloud resources requires extra coordination.
- Emergency response can conflict with default deny. Incident responders often need broad access quickly. A break-glass role must be separate from daily roles. The role must expire automatically.

These points show that zero trust reduces some risks and adds new operational requirements. It is not a product that an organization installs once. It is an operating model that requires continuous maintenance.

OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a standard identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0. OAuth 2.0 lets an application get delegated access to a user's resources. OAuth 2.0 alone does not tell the application who the user is. OpenID Connect adds an ID token to solve this problem. The ID token is a signed JSON Web Token. It contains claims about the user and the authentication event.

Three parties take part in an OpenID Connect transaction.
- End-User: the person who wants to sign in to an application.
- Relying Party (RP): the application or website that needs to know the user's identity, also called the client.
- OpenID Provider (OP): the service that authenticates the End-User and issues tokens, also called the identity provider.

A typical authorization code flow has these steps.
1. The End-User starts at the RP.
2. The RP redirects the browser to the OP authorization endpoint with a request that includes client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code, scope=openid, state, and nonce.
3. The OP authenticates the End-User and obtains consent.
4. The OP redirects the browser back to the RP with an authorization code and the same state value.
5. The RP sends the authorization code to the OP token endpoint with its client credentials.
6. The OP returns an ID token, an access token, and a refresh token if the RP requests offline access.
7. The RP verifies the ID token signature, issuer, audience, nonce, and expiration time.
8. The RP can call the OP UserInfo endpoint with the access token to get more user claims.

The RP fetches the OP public keys from the OP JSON Web Key Set document to verify the signature. The RP verifies the state value to prevent authorization code injection. The RP verifies the nonce to prevent replay of old ID tokens. The ID token is for the RP. The access token is for the OP UserInfo endpoint or other APIs. A client must not use an ID token as an access token.

Because many RPs can use the same OP, the End-User can sign in once at the OP. Then each RP can get its own ID token after a redirect. This setup enables single sign-on across different applications. The RP does not see the End-User's password. The OP keeps the password.

Open-loop control is appropriate when these conditions are true:
- The process is stable.
- Disturbances are small or known.
- The output tolerance is wide.

If one condition is false, closed-loop control is the better choice.

Stability comparison:
- Open-loop control cannot cause instability from a feedback loop.
- Open-loop control does not correct a process that is already unstable.
- Closed-loop control can correct some unstable processes.
- If the controller gain is too high, closed-loop control can oscillate or become unstable.

Cost comparison:
- Open-loop control costs less than closed-loop control.
- Open-loop control does not need a sensor.
- Open-loop control does not need feedback wiring.
- Open-loop control does not need a complex controller.
- Closed-loop control costs more than open-loop control.
- Closed-loop control needs sensors.
- Closed-loop control needs amplifiers.
- Closed-loop control needs a more capable controller.
- If the process changes, open-loop control can require manual recalibration.

Complexity comparison:
- Open-loop control is simpler to design and install.
- Open-loop control is simpler to maintain.
- You must know the process gain and disturbance limits.
- Closed-loop control is more complex.
- Closed-loop control needs a plant model.
- Closed-loop control needs a tuned controller.
- Closed-loop control needs validation tests.

Suitability:
- Open-loop control suits processes with constant load and slow drift.
- A fixed-speed conveyor is an example if its load stays near constant.
- Closed-loop control suits processes with variable load.
- Closed-loop control suits processes with strong disturbances.
- Closed-loop control suits processes with strict accuracy requirements.
- Temperature control of a reactor and flow control in a chemical feed line are examples.

No, that view is not accurate. These tactical patterns include entities and value objects. They also include repositories. But tactical patterns are only one level of DDD. The other level is strategic design. Some teams ignore the strategic level.

Strategic design starts with a ubiquitous language. The team builds this language with domain experts. The same terms appear in code and in conversations. This shared language keeps the model aligned with the business.

Bounded contexts give each model a clear boundary. A term can represent different concepts in different contexts. The context map records the relations between the contexts. These maps guide how teams integrate their software.

Subdomain analysis separates the core domain from other subdomains. The core domain gives the business a competitive advantage. The team must focus most of its effort on the core domain. Subdomains that support the core domain are necessary but do not differentiate the business. Generic subdomains can use solutions that already exist.

In practice, the strategic side matters for large systems. Multiple teams often own different bounded contexts. If context maps are not explicit, teams duplicate models and create inconsistent integration points. Strategic design also helps when a legacy system constrains the new design. An anticorruption layer protects a new context from a legacy model.

Tactical patterns operate inside a bounded context. They express the model in code. They do not replace strategic decisions. Teams must decide the boundaries before they choose entities and repositories.

DDD is not a universal solution. Simple applications with little business complexity do not need full strategic design. A small team that writes a single application can use tactical patterns alone. For complex domains with many teams, the strategic side is essential.

Effective instructions have these qualities:
- Correct
- Findable
- Actionable
- Safe

Principles:
- Write one action per step.
- Put conditions before commands.
- State the expected result after each action.
- Add a verification step after a block of steps.
- Add a warning before any destructive action.
- Keep procedural text separate from descriptive text.
- Use the same word for the same meaning throughout the document.

Structure of steps:
1. Start with prerequisites.
2. Number each action in the correct order.
3. Keep each step as one imperative sentence.
4. Put any condition before the action.
5. Show the expected result after each action.
6. End with a verification procedure.

Conditional paths:
Use an if-then structure. State the condition first. Put alternative paths in separate numbered or lettered branches. Label each branch clearly. Do not nest more than two levels. For example, write "If the test fails, read the log." This structure keeps a branch that fails separate. Each branch must show how to return to the main sequence.

Numbered lists versus prose:
Numbered lists suit these items:
- Sequential actions
- Commands
- Steps that must not be skipped
Prose suits these items:
- Concepts
- Background
- Prerequisites
- Warnings
A mixed format is effective. Use prose for context before a numbered procedure. Use numbered lists for the procedure itself.

A list makes a sequence easy to scan and check. Prose can explain why a step exists, but long prose inside a procedure reduces readability. Detailed explanations belong in notes, not inside the steps.

Trade-offs for different audiences:
Expert users prefer short numbered lists with minimal explanation. Novice users need the following:
- More prose
- Definitions
- Expected outputs
- Error recovery
For a mixed audience, write concise numbered steps. Put details in notes or expandable sections. Too many conditional branches reduce readability. When possible, use one branch per reader role. Verify each branch with a separate test.

1. Identify the source pod, the destination pod, and their namespaces.
2. Check that your CNI enforces Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. See the CNI documentation for your version.
3. List all NetworkPolicy objects in each namespace. Use kubectl get networkpolicies -n <namespace>.
4. Get the labels of the source and destination pods. Use kubectl get pods -n <namespace> --show-labels. Check all replicas. A label mismatch on one replica can cause intermittent failures.
5. Get the labels of the namespaces. Use kubectl get namespaces --show-labels.
6. In the destination pod namespace, find each NetworkPolicy that selects the destination pod. Compare the policy podSelector with the destination pod labels.
7. In the source pod namespace, find each NetworkPolicy that selects the source pod for egress. Compare the policy podSelector with the source pod labels.
8. Check the policyTypes field in each relevant policy. If the field is empty, apply these defaults. A policy with no rules defaults to Ingress only. A policy with only egress rules defaults to Ingress and Egress. A policy with only ingress rules defaults to Ingress only. A policy with both rule types defaults to Ingress and Egress. After you determine policyTypes, check the direction. If Ingress is not in policyTypes, the policy does not restrict ingress. If Egress is not in policyTypes, the policy does not restrict egress.
9. For each policy with Ingress, read the ingress rules. For each rule, check the from fields.
10. For each policy with Egress, read the egress rules. For each rule, check the to fields.
11. For each ingress rule, check the from fields. A podSelector selects pods in the same namespace as the NetworkPolicy. A namespaceSelector selects namespaces by labels. If both are present, the source pod must match the podSelector and its namespace must match the namespaceSelector.
12. For each egress rule, check the to fields. A podSelector selects pods in the same namespace as the NetworkPolicy. A namespaceSelector selects namespaces by labels. If both are present, the destination pod must match the podSelector and its namespace must match the namespaceSelector.
13. Check rule interactions within a policy. In an ingress rule, all from entries combine with OR. In an egress rule, all to entries combine with OR. In one entry, the podSelector and namespaceSelector combine with AND.
14. Check interactions across policies. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules are additive. If any policy allows the connection, the CNI allows the connection. If no policy allows the connection, the CNI denies it. This applies only when at least one policy selects the pod for that direction.
15. If no NetworkPolicy selects the pod, the pod is not isolated. The CNI allows all traffic to and from that pod.
16. Check for a default deny policy. If a default deny policy exists for a direction, traffic in that direction must match an explicit allow rule.
17. Check for CNI-specific custom resources. Some CNIs, such as Calico and Cilium, enforce their own policy types in addition to Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Review those resources too.
18. Check the CNI logs for denied flows. Set the CNI log level to debug if needed. See the CNI documentation for the correct command.
19. Reproduce the connection with a test pod. Run a connection test from the source pod to the destination service. Use a tool such as curl or nc.
20. Before you change any policy, save its current YAML.
21. After you change any policy, wait for the CNI to apply the change. Then test again.
22. Roll back any change that does not fix the problem.

1. The transit provider sends a BGP UPDATE that contains a prefix and one or more community tags.
2. Apply the inbound BGP route policy to the eBGP session.
3. The policy matches the community tags in the UPDATE.
4. The policy sets the local preference for the route.
5. If more than one policy term matches, the first matching term sets the value.
6. Store the received route in the Adj-RIB-In before policy.
7. Apply the policy to the route attributes.
8. Put the modified route in the Loc-RIB.
9. Run the BGP decision process for all paths that have the same prefix.
10. Compare the local preference values early in the process.
11. Select the best path.
12. Install the best path in the main RIB if the route is valid and no other routing protocol has a better administrative distance.
13. For overlapping prefixes, treat each prefix as a separate route.
14. Do not inherit community or local preference from a less specific prefix.
15. Attach the community to each prefix that needs the local preference.
16. If the same prefix comes from multiple transit providers, set local preference for each path.
17. Select one best path for the prefix.
18. If BGP multipath is enabled and the paths are equal, more than one path can enter the RIB.
19. Advertise the selected route to the iBGP peers.
20. If the iBGP peers cannot reach the original next hop, configure next-hop-self on the eBGP speaker.
21. The route reflector receives the route.
22. A route reflector with no inbound policy does not change the local preference.
23. Run the BGP decision process on the route reflector.
24. Reflect the best path to the route reflector clients.
25. Add the route reflector cluster ID to the cluster list.
26. A client receives the reflected route.
27. Apply the client inbound policy.
28. Run the BGP decision process on the client.
29. Install the selected best path in the client RIB.

Main operational causes vary by city and by carrier. The causes that follow are common in dense urban areas.

- High traffic congestion on narrow streets during business hours.
- Limited legal parking near the delivery address.
- Gated building access and restricted freight entrances.
- A large number of stops for each driver in a short period.
- Incomplete or incorrect address data.
- The recipient is not available during the delivery window.

Delivery windows create a hard time limit for the first attempt. Traffic, parking, or access delays can consume the window. Address quality controls how fast the driver finds the correct door. A missing unit number or an incorrect geo-code can send the driver to the wrong location. The driver loses time and often cannot return within the window. In many networks, a failed first attempt can convert the shipment to a next-day retry.

A promised time can allow only one attempt in many delivery networks. Bad address data reduces the time that remains within the window. A failed first attempt occurs when the window closes before delivery or when the recipient is absent. These three factors are cumulative. A short window leaves little tolerance for address correction or recovery from a failed attempt. This combination can push the shipment past its promised time.

The todo list shows `noop` when the rebase range contains no commits. The range is the set of commits reachable from HEAD but not from the base. This happens when the base equals HEAD or is a descendant of HEAD. A default rebase uses the upstream branch. If the current branch has no commits ahead of the upstream, the range is empty.

Checks

1. Check the current branch status. Run `git status` and `git branch -vv`.
2. Confirm the ahead count. If the ahead count is zero, the default rebase has no commits to apply.
3. List recent commits. Run `git log --oneline -n 10`.
4. Identify the parent of the oldest commit that you want to change.
5. Start the rebase with an explicit base. Use a commit before that parent. For example, run `git rebase -i HEAD~3` for the last three commits.
6. If the commits go back to the initial commit, run `git rebase -i --root`.
7. After the editor opens, confirm that the todo list contains `pick` lines for your commits.
8. If the list still shows only `noop`, abort the rebase. Run `git rebase --abort`. Then check the base argument again.

Layer 4 and layer 7 load balancers differ in session affinity and in the three requested areas.

Latency

A layer 4 load balancer forwards TCP packets and adds little delay. It does not parse HTTP or wait for the full request. A layer 7 load balancer waits for the HTTP headers before it selects a backend. It decrypts TLS and parses HTTP, which adds more delay. Both load balancers perform TLS handshake and encryption work when they terminate TLS. The extra delay from layer 7 is small compared to network delay for most web services.

Observability

A layer 4 load balancer sees these items:
- source IP
- destination IP
- ports
- byte counts
- connection duration

It cannot read these items:
- HTTP status codes
- cookies
- paths

It can see TLS version and cipher if it terminates TLS. A layer 7 load balancer sees the full HTTP request and response after TLS termination. It can log these items:
- session IDs
- status codes
- per-request latency

The layer 7 load balancer gives better data to find the cause of session loss.

Failover behavior

A layer 4 load balancer uses TCP health checks. It can send traffic to a backend that accepts TCP but returns HTTP errors. When a backend fails, the load balancer can reset existing connections. The client must reconnect. The client loses session state unless the backends share it.

A layer 7 load balancer uses HTTP health checks. It can stop traffic to a failing backend before clients see errors. It can return a clear HTTP error or retry a request to another backend. For session affinity, the layer 7 load balancer can send the client to a new backend and set a new cookie. The new backend starts a new session unless the backends share session state. The layer 4 load balancer cannot do this because it cannot read the session cookie.

Session affinity

The layer 4 load balancer can attach a client by source IP. This method fails when clients use network address translation or change networks. The layer 7 load balancer can attach a client by a cookie or a header. This method survives IP changes. The layer 7 load balancer can read the session cookie because it terminates TLS. The layer 7 method is more reliable for session continuity.

Confidence intervals and prediction intervals answer different questions. A confidence interval estimates an unknown fixed quantity, such as the true average commute time over many days. A prediction interval estimates one future value, such as the commute time on one specific day.

For the average commute time, a 95% confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the true average. A statistical method builds a 95% confidence interval. In about 95% of repeated samples from the same process, that method includes the true average. It does not give a 95% probability that this specific interval contains the true average. The width of the interval comes mainly from the amount of sample data. More data give a narrower interval.

For one day's commute, a 95% prediction interval gives a range of plausible values for that single day. This interval must cover two sources of variation. One source is that the data do not reveal the true average exactly. The other source is day-to-day variation around that average. Traffic, weather, or other events can make an individual commute much longer or shorter than average.

For the same 95% level and the same model, the prediction interval is wider than the confidence interval. The prediction interval includes both sources of variation. The confidence interval includes only the first source. The two intervals become the same only if individual daily commutes have no random variation around the average. For commute times, that condition does not hold.

Both intervals assume that the data are a random sample from the same process. If the process changes, the intervals are not valid for the new process.

A permutation is an arrangement where the order of the chosen items counts. A combination is a selection where the order of the chosen items does not count.

In this example, you have five distinct books on a shelf. You choose three books to read in a specific order. The sequence Book A, Book B, Book C is different from Book C, Book B, Book A. That is a permutation. You choose three books to donate. The set of Book A, Book B, Book C is the same as Book C, Book B, Book A. That is a combination.

Order matters when the position or sequence is part of the outcome. Examples are race results, passwords, and book order. Order does not matter when only the chosen group matters. Examples are donation sets and committee membership.

The formulas apply to n distinct items when you choose r items without repetition.

For permutations:
P(n, r) = n! / (n - r)!

For combinations:
C(n, r) = n! / (r! (n - r)!)

For the same n and r, the number of permutations equals the number of combinations multiplied by r!. For each chosen set of r items, r! different orders exist. The combination formula divides by r! to count each set once.

For five books and three chosen books, the values are:
P(5,3) = 60
C(5,3) = 10

Severity and Priority in Issue Triage

Severity is a technical measure. It describes the effect of a defect on system function, data, security, or compliance. It answers this question: How bad is the effect? Severity does not change with business schedules.

Priority is a work-order measure. It describes the sequence for resolution work. Priority combines severity with business factors. These factors include:

- user exposure
- reproduction rate
- release constraints
- workarounds
- service-level agreements

The two dimensions diverge when probability, exposure, or business constraints change. Severity stays with the defect. Priority changes with context.

Case 1: High severity with a very low reproduction rate

A defect that can cause data loss has high severity. If the defect reproduces only in rare conditions, its priority can be lower than another high-severity defect that reproduces often. The severity remains high because the potential damage is high. You must not ignore the defect. You can add an alert for the rare trigger condition. If the probability is low and a workaround exists, you can set the priority lower.

Case 2: Low severity cosmetic defect that blocks a critical release

A cosmetic defect has low severity. It does not cause data loss or an outage. If the defect blocks a critical release, its priority becomes high. You must start the work immediately to remove the release blocker. Priority rises because of the business deadline, not because of the technical effect. This is a divergence of low severity and high priority.

How to set the two dimensions

Use these rules to set the dimensions:

- Set severity from the technical effect only.
- Do not change severity when a release deadline approaches.
- Set priority as the work sequence.
- When a defect blocks a release or affects many users, you can raise priority.
- When a high-severity defect has a very low reproduction rate and a safe workaround exists, you can lower priority.
- Record the reason for the divergence in the ticket.

The two dimensions must stay independent. You must not use severity as the only input for priority.

- Keep ethanol containers closed when you do not use them.
- Store ethanol in a flammables storage cabinet.
- Dispose of ethanol waste in a designated flammable solvent container.
- Do not pour ethanol down the sink or drain.
- Wash your hands after you handle ethanol.

Check these items:

- Check the pipette tip for cracks or damage. Replace a damaged tip.
- Check that the tip fits tightly on the pipette. A loose tip causes air leaks.
- Use tips that are made for your pipette model.
- Check the pipette seals and O-rings for wear. Replace worn parts.
- Calibrate the pipette with ethanol at 100 µL.
- Pre-wet the tip with ethanol before each series of measurements.
- Aspirate ethanol slowly. Fast aspiration can create air bubbles.
- Hold the pipette vertically during aspiration.
- Immerse the tip 2 mm to 4 mm below the liquid surface.
- After aspiration, wait 1 to 2 seconds before you remove the tip from the liquid.
- Dispense against the container wall and touch off the last drop.
- Use reverse pipetting for ethanol. Press to the second stop before aspiration. Dispense to the first stop. Discard the residual liquid.

Here are common errors in the format of the Authorization header and in the way the token is encoded. These errors can cause a 401 response even when the token is valid. The exact behavior depends on the server implementation. Most servers follow RFC 6750.

- The header lacks a space between the scheme and the token. The correct format is "Bearer <token>".
- The scheme uses lowercase or mixed case. Some servers require exactly "Bearer".
- The header contains extra spaces or tabs before the scheme or after the token.
- The header contains a line break. The header value must be on one line.
- The header includes single or double quotation marks around the token. Quotation marks are not part of the format.
- The header includes percent-encoded or HTML-encoded characters. The server expects the raw token characters.
- The header includes a prefix such as "Token:" or "Bearer:" after the scheme. The format uses only a space.
- The token contains characters that RFC 6750 does not allow. Permitted characters include letters, digits, and - . _ ~ + / =.
- The client sends more than one Authorization header. The server can reject duplicate headers.
- A proxy or gateway changes or removes the header. The server then returns 401.

These errors can cause a 401 response if the server rejects the header format. Many servers follow RFC 6750, but individual implementations differ.

Before the project starts, obtain the course roster and the institution's audit policy.

Complete these steps:
1. Write a project plan. Include a list of roles, tasks, milestones, and individual assessment criteria.
2. Assign one role to each registered student. Give the same role list to all group members.
3. Require each student to sign the project plan. Keep a copy for your records.
4. Hold a short meeting each week. Ask each student to report tasks that they completed.
5. Update a contribution log after each meeting. The log must record tasks and the student who completed them.
6. Check the log at three fixed points. If the log shows less work for a student than the plan, meet that student.
7. If one student does much more work than others, reassign part of their tasks to balance the load.
8. After the group submits the joint deliverable, require each student to submit an individual report. This report must identify the student's own work and the work of other members.
9. Hold an individual oral examination for each student about the joint deliverable. Ask questions that require understanding of all parts, not only the student's own part.
10. Compare the contribution log to the individual report and the oral exam answers. Award a separate grade for individual mastery. Do not use only the group grade.

If a student withdraws, do these steps:
11. Remove the withdrawn student from the project plan.
12. Assign their remaining tasks to the other members. Adjust the contribution log.
13. Do not penalize the other members for incomplete work that the withdrawn student caused.

If a student audits the course, do these steps:
14. Tell the audit student at the start that they will not receive a letter grade.
15. Require the audit student to complete the same role tasks. Record participation in the contribution log.

If a group splits because of interpersonal conflict, do these steps:
16. Split the group into two new subgroups. Adjust the deliverable scope for each subgroup.
17. Assign new roles in each subgroup. Update the contribution log. Update the assessment plan.
18. Require each subgroup to submit a separate version of the joint deliverable. Grade each subgroup separately.

PostgreSQL Isolation Levels Under MVCC

PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control (MVCC). Each transaction reads a snapshot of committed data. The snapshot timing defines the isolation level. The default isolation level is READ COMMITTED.

Isolation levels:

- READ COMMITTED
Each statement sees the latest committed row version at the start of that statement.
It prevents dirty reads only.
It does not prevent non-repeatable reads.
It does not prevent phantom reads.
It does not prevent serialization anomalies.

- REPEATABLE READ
The transaction uses one snapshot from the first statement in that transaction.
It prevents dirty reads.
It prevents non-repeatable reads.
It prevents phantom reads.
It does not prevent serialization anomalies.

- SERIALIZABLE
The transaction uses one snapshot and detects conflicts with serializable snapshot isolation (SSI).
It prevents dirty reads.
It prevents non-repeatable reads.
It prevents phantom reads.
It prevents serialization anomalies.

Edge cases:

Write skew is a serialization anomaly. Two transactions read the same predicate and update different rows based on that predicate. For example, two doctors are on call. A rule requires at least one doctor on call. Each transaction reads the count of on-call doctors and finds two. Then each transaction sets a different doctor off call. Under REPEATABLE READ, both transactions can commit. The resulting state has zero doctors on call. This state does not match any serial order. In a serial order, the second transaction sees the first update. SERIALIZABLE detects this conflict. PostgreSQL aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001.

Predicate locks:

SERIALIZABLE uses predicate locks. Predicate locks record the rows or index ranges that a transaction reads. They detect conflicts from read predicates that overlap when write sets do not overlap. This mechanism prevents phantom reads and write skew. It can increase abort rates for long transactions and for workloads with many overlapping reads.

High-concurrency behavior:

Under high concurrency, SERIALIZABLE transactions can abort more often. Application code must retry the transaction after SQLSTATE 40001. REPEATABLE READ does not require retry for that error. It does not guarantee serializability. A read-only SERIALIZABLE transaction can also receive SQLSTATE 40001. SERIALIZABLE is necessary for write skew prevention.

In a matrixed software organization, no uniform model defines these roles. The description below applies to a common implementation. Functional managers own people and capacity. Product managers own product value. Program managers own cross-team delivery plans. Project managers own work execution within a defined scope.

Decision rights when a release slips

- The product manager decides which scope to defer. The product manager approves trade-offs between scope, schedule, and quality. The product manager cannot direct engineering capacity in a weak matrix.
- The program manager owns the release plan across teams. The program manager decides the sequence and the dependency adjustments. The program manager proposes the revised date when the slip occurs. The program manager cannot decide product scope without product manager approval.
