For this write-heavy, time-series workload, the main choice is between range partitioning on the timestamp and hash partitioning on a high-cardinality key. List partitioning is less suitable because event timestamps are continuous and unbounded.

Range partitioning on the timestamp puts every new row in the latest partition. That partition becomes the single hot partition for all inserts. Contention on this partition can limit write throughput. Hash partitioning spreads rows evenly across partitions when the hash key has high cardinality. It avoids a single hot partition and gives better parallel insert performance.

List partitioning on a continuous timestamp is not practical because you must enumerate values. If you convert timestamps into fixed buckets such as week numbers, list partitioning sends all current writes to one bucket. That creates the same hotspot as range partitioning.

Range partitioning gives the best pruning for scans over recent timestamps. The query reads only the partitions that overlap the requested time range. Hash partitioning prevents pruning by timestamp. The query must scan all partitions because consecutive timestamps hash to different partitions. This is true for a hash key on the timestamp and for any other hash key. List partitioning prunes only when the query names the exact bucket values. A continuous time range across many buckets still scans all overlapping buckets.

Range partitioning aligns with time-based retention. You can add future partitions ahead of time or use automatic partition creation. You can drop old partitions when you delete old data. Hash partitioning normally uses a fixed number of partitions. When you add or remove partitions, the operation causes expensive data movement. List partitioning needs manual work for every new bucket value. A time-series table produces new timestamp values forever, so list maintenance is continuous.

For this workload, range partitioning gives fast occasional range scans but a hot latest partition and partition management. Hash partitioning gives balanced inserts but slow timestamp range scans. List partitioning is not a practical choice for continuous event timestamps. It is useful only when the time dimension is a small fixed set of buckets.

An API gateway must forward streaming response chunks as they arrive. The gateway must not buffer the entire payload. For HTTP/1.1, the gateway must use chunked transfer encoding. For HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the gateway must use data frames and flow control. The gateway must apply backpressure when the client reads slower than the upstream sends. The gateway must disable response body aggregation.

The gateway must set per-stream read and write timeouts. A long silence between chunks must not close the connection prematurely. The gateway can use an idle timeout but must reset it on each chunk. The gateway must not apply response body size limits to a streaming response.

After a WebSocket upgrade request, the gateway must forward the Upgrade and Connection headers. The gateway must validate the origin and the requested subprotocol. After the backend returns status 101, the gateway must establish a bidirectional tunnel. The gateway must not parse or buffer WebSocket frames. It must forward bytes in both directions and enforce backpressure. The gateway must set an idle timeout and a maximum connection lifetime.

The gateway must not count ping or pong frames as data for rate limiting. The gateway must forward close frames and allow the endpoints to complete the closing handshake. The gateway must not apply HTTP request or response body size limits after the upgrade.

For long-polling, the gateway must hold the request open until the backend sends a response or a timeout expires. The gateway must not buffer the response before the backend sends it. The gateway must return the backend response as soon as it arrives. The gateway must treat a long-poll timeout as a normal empty response or a client retry signal. The gateway must use a separate timeout for long-polling that is longer than the normal request timeout. The gateway must not count the waiting period as request processing time.

Rate limiting can cause problems in these modes. A per-request counter that expires before the stream ends can allow more concurrent streams than intended. A rate limiter that counts each chunk as a request can block a stream after the first chunk. A byte-based token bucket can starve a long-lived connection if the refill rate is too low.

The gateway must distinguish connection establishment from ongoing transfer. For WebSockets, rate limiting must apply to connection attempts and message counts, not to raw frame counts. For long-polling, rate limiting must not punish clients that hold a connection to wait for an event.

A circuit breaker that opens based on total request latency will treat all long-polling requests as failures. This happens if the latency threshold is lower than the poll timeout. A circuit breaker that counts timeouts as errors will open during normal long-polling activity. A circuit breaker that samples only the first bytes of a stream can miss upstream failures that occur later. For streaming, a circuit breaker must remain closed while bytes flow even if the total time is long. The gateway must use error rate and explicit failure signals, not wall-clock duration, for circuit breaker decisions on streaming and long-polling connections.

The gateway must distinguish expected long-poll timeouts from upstream errors such as connection refused, reset, or status 5xx. The gateway must support a half-open state with one trial connection per upstream. The half-open probe can send a small request and check the initial response.

No. Interactive rebase does not always make a shared branch unsafe. It rewrites commit hashes for the replayed commits and all subsequent commits. It does not change commits before the rebase point. The danger applies only after other people base their work on the rewritten commits.

Safe patterns include:

- A safe pattern is to rebase local commits before the first push to a remote branch. No other person has these commits, so the rewrite is safe.
- A safe pattern is to use interactive rebase on a feature branch that only you work on. You can then use the command `git push --force-with-lease` to replace the remote branch.
- A use of interactive rebase on a shared integration branch such as `main` or `develop` is not safe. Other people depend on those commits.
- If multiple people work on the same feature branch, they must agree on a rebase point in advance. They must not rebase after they share the branch.

`--force-with-lease` is not a license to rewrite shared history. It only fails if the remote branch has commits that you did not fetch. Other people can still have local work based on the old commits. Other people with local copies must then reset their branches to the new history.

Rotor slot skew is a helical displacement of the rotor slots along the shaft. It spreads each rotor bar over the skew angle. This spread reduces the magnetic interaction between stator and rotor slot permeance harmonics. The reduced interaction lowers torque ripple. A typical skew angle equals one stator slot pitch. In an ideal linear model, that angle cancels the first stator slot permeance harmonic.

Slot harmonics produce asynchronous parasitic torques. Some stator and rotor slot harmonic pairs produce synchronous parasitic torques. These torques appear as cusps in the torque-speed curve. Skew reduces the amplitude of these harmonic fields. It thus reduces the cusps and the associated torque ripple. Under low-slip conditions, the rotor currents have a low fundamental frequency.

The slot harmonics induce rotor currents that produce torque ripple. Skew reduces these harmonic currents near synchronous speed. The result is smoother torque at low slip. High-order harmonic interactions occur between stator and rotor slot harmonic orders. The skew factor describes the reduction of a harmonic due to skew. A skew angle can set the skew factor to zero for one chosen slot harmonic and thus cancel that harmonic.

The same skew does not cancel all stator and rotor slot harmonics at once. It can reduce many high-order interactions to low values. Skew adds a small rotor leakage reactance and reduces the fundamental torque slightly.

A tail call is a function call that occurs as the last action of a function. The caller returns the result of that call directly. No work remains after the call returns. Scheme standards require proper tail recursion. This requirement lets tail calls use a constant amount of stack space.

Follow these steps to rewrite a simple recursive function into tail-recursive form.

1. Identify the recursive call that is not in tail position.
2. Add an accumulator parameter to the function.
3. Change the base case to return the accumulator value.
4. Change the recursive case to update the accumulator before the recursive call.
5. Call the helper function with the initial accumulator value.

Example for a factorial function.

Non-tail-recursive version:

(define (factorial n)
  (if (= n 0)
      1
      (* n (factorial (- n 1)))))

Tail-recursive version:

(define (factorial n)
  (define (iter n acc)
    (if (= n 0)
        acc
        (iter (- n 1) (* n acc))))
  (iter n 1))

Verify the new function with small inputs. Compare the results with the original function. If the results differ, correct the accumulator update.

These three architectures differ in package structure, component communication, and deployment method.

The effects for a small team are different for each architecture.

- A monolith is one deployable unit. All features share one codebase and one process. Development speed can be high at the start. Deployment is one artifact. Long-term maintenance can become difficult if the code is not modular. The failure of one part can stop the whole application.

- A service-oriented architecture (SOA) uses separate services that communicate through an enterprise service bus. This design adds middleware, governance, and standard protocols such as SOAP. Development speed can be slower because the team must manage the bus and service contracts. Deployment can be complex. Long-term maintenance can depend on that shared infrastructure. This architecture usually fits large enterprises, not small teams.

- Microservices are separate deployable units. Each service owns its data and communicates over network protocols. Development speed can be slower at the start because the team must manage many services and network failures. Deployment can require multiple pipelines and coordination. Long-term maintenance can isolate changes, but operational overhead can be high.

For a small team, a modular monolith can give the fastest start and the simplest deployment. The team can split the monolith later if the application grows. The choice depends on the team's operations skills and the expected growth.

The statement is not correct. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) can use metric types other than CPU and memory.

The HPA supports these metric types:
- Resource metrics include CPU and memory for pods.
- Pods metrics include custom metrics for each pod, for example request latency.
- Object metrics include custom metrics for a Kubernetes object, for example queue depth per service.
- External metrics include metrics from outside the cluster, for example queue depth in a cloud queue.

To use custom or external metrics, you must deploy an adapter that implements the custom.metrics.k8s.io API, the external.metrics.k8s.io API, or both. Common adapters include Prometheus Adapter and KEDA. The adapter reads metrics from a monitoring system such as Prometheus or a cloud monitoring service.

The HPA configuration includes a metrics field. This field defines the metric type, metric name, and target value. The metric type can be Pods, Object, or External.

Start with Ampère's law without displacement current. The line integral around a loop equals μ0 times the enclosed conduction current. For a loop around the wire that feeds one plate, the surface through the wire gives I. For a surface that passes between the plates, no conduction current crosses. Thus the same loop gives two different results. This contradiction disappears when Maxwell adds the displacement current term ε0 dΦ_E/dt. Between the plates, the electric flux increases. The derivative ε0 dΦ_E/dt equals the conduction current I that charges the capacitor. The corrected law is: ∮ B·dl = μ0(I_enc + ε0 dΦ_E/dt). On the surface between the plates, I_enc = 0 and the displacement term gives μ0 I. The result matches the surface through the wire.

Assume circular plates of radius R. Consider a loop of radius r < R, centered on the axis. Assume that the electric field E is uniform between the plates. The enclosed electric flux is Φ_E = E πr^2. The corrected law gives B 2πr = μ0 ε0 πr^2 dE/dt. Therefore B = (μ0 ε0 r/2) dE/dt inside the plates. If I is the charging current and the field is uniform, I = ε0 πR^2 dE/dt. Then B = μ0 I r /(2πR^2). The field lines are circles around the axis. The direction follows the right-hand rule for the displacement current. These results ignore fringing fields at the plate edges.

## Diagnose the pattern

Use these steps.

1. Check the consumer source code. Find the offset commit call and the side effect calls.
2. Write the order of these calls.
3. If the commit precedes the side effects, record the crash window.
4. Search the logs for events that ran more than once.
5. Check each side effect store for absent rows, files, or external calls.
6. If you can use a test environment, reproduce the crash there. Stop the process after the commit and before the side effects. Inspect the state.

## Compare fixes

### Idempotent consumer

An idempotent consumer checks a unique message identifier before it starts the side effects. The consumer skips the event if the identifier exists. The consumer stores the identifier after the side effects finish. This approach removes duplicates only when the side effects and the identifier store share one transaction. Otherwise a crash between the side effects and the identifier store can repeat the work.

### Transactional outbox

The consumer writes the side effects and an outbox event in one database transaction. The consumer commits the offset after that transaction commits. A separate publisher reads the outbox and sends events. This fix prevents missed side effects when the crash occurs after the commit. A crash before the offset commit repeats the event, so the consumer must be idempotent. It does not make external systems atomic unless they join the same transaction.

### Manual offset commits

In manual offset commit mode, the consumer commits the offset after the side effects finish. This order reduces missed work. A crash before the commit repeats the event. The consumer must be idempotent to handle the repeated event. Manual commits do not coordinate external side effects.

Likely causes:

- The election timeout is too short for the network latency. A follower starts a new election when it does not receive a heartbeat before the timeout. This condition occurs often if the timeout is shorter than the round-trip time.
- The heartbeat interval is too long. If the heartbeat interval is larger than the election timeout, followers can time out before they receive any heartbeat. The leader can lose leadership even when it is healthy.
- The quorum size is too large for the number of reachable voter nodes. A candidate must receive votes from a majority of the voter nodes to win an election. If the number of reachable nodes is smaller than the quorum size, no candidate can win. Repeated elections follow.
- The randomization range for the election timeout is too narrow. All nodes can start elections at the same time when the timeout expires. This causes split votes and repeated elections.
- In many Raft implementations, the quorum size is a function of the voter membership. It is not a separate setting. Misconfiguration can occur in the list of voter nodes.

Diagnosis procedure:

Prerequisite: You must have access to cluster logs, metrics, and configuration files.

1. Check the election timeout value in each node configuration.
2. Measure the maximum network round-trip time between nodes under high latency.
3. Check whether the election timeout is shorter than the maximum round-trip time.
4. If the election timeout is shorter, increase the election timeout on all nodes.
5. Check the heartbeat interval value in each node configuration.
6. Check whether the heartbeat interval is greater than or equal to the election timeout.
7. If the heartbeat interval is too large, set the heartbeat interval to a value smaller than the election timeout.
8. Check the list of voter nodes and the quorum size setting.
9. Check whether the number of reachable voter nodes is smaller than the quorum size.
10. If the number of reachable voter nodes is smaller than the quorum size, restore connectivity to the unreachable nodes.
11. If you cannot restore connectivity and the unreachable nodes are permanently failed, remove the unreachable voters from the membership.
12. Check the randomization range for the election timeout.
13. If the randomization range is too narrow, increase the range.
14. Check the logs for repeated election terms without a leader.
15. If repeated elections continue after these changes, check for network partition or firewall rules.

Warning: Do not remove voter nodes during a network partition. Removal can cause data loss.

Code review tools mark comments in two ways.

A comment that blocks prevents the merge or the approval until the author resolves it. A comment that does not block records a suggestion or a question. The author can merge without resolving that comment.

The exact rules vary by team and tool. In a typical workflow, the following findings are blockers:

- A security vulnerability that an attacker can exploit is a blocker.
- A defect that causes data loss, data corruption, or a crash is a blocker.
- Logic that violates an explicit requirement or an acceptance criterion is a blocker.
- An API change that breaks a consumer without a migration path is a blocker.
- A race condition, a deadlock, or a resource leak is a blocker.
- The absence of tests for new critical behavior or for a fixed defect is a blocker.
- A performance regression that exceeds a defined threshold is a blocker.
- A failure to comply with legal or regulatory requirements is a blocker.
- Code that handles errors incorrectly and can corrupt data or mask a failure is a blocker.

These items block because the cost of a merge with them is high. Most other comments are suggestions.

# Investigation procedure

1. Check the available metrics from the producer, the consumer, and the connectors.
2. Check the producer send path for unbounded buffers or queues.
3. Check each stage between the consumer and the producer for asynchronous boundaries.
4. Check that the consumer pause action propagates to the producer.
5. Check connector settings for disabled flow control.
6. Check serialization and deserialization buffers for unbounded growth.
7. Check network and protocol buffers for extra queues.
8. Check batch processing before the producer for record accumulation.
9. Check checkpoint intervals and state flush timing for delayed acknowledgments.
10. Check logs and metrics for dropped or delayed pause signals.
11. Check input and output rates at each stage for imbalance.
12. Run a controlled burst test in a test environment to isolate the stage with weak backpressure.

# Comparison

The exact behavior depends on the streaming framework and its connectors.

Credit-based flow control gives credits from the consumer to the producer. The producer sends messages only while credits remain. This method prevents producer buffer growth when the consumer stops credit grants. It requires flow control support at every stage. Credit granularity affects throughput and latency.

Load shedding drops new messages when a component is overloaded. This method keeps memory and latency bounded under burst load. It causes data loss because some messages do not reach the consumer. It is useful when freshness matters more than completeness. The system uses a policy to select messages for drop.

Adaptive batching changes the batch size or batch delay based on load. Larger batches increase throughput but can increase latency. Smaller batches reduce latency but can reduce throughput. This method does not give a memory bound by itself. Without credit-based flow control or load shedding, batch buffers can still grow.

Credit-based flow control gives the strongest memory bound. Load shedding accepts data loss in exchange for that bound. Adaptive batching improves efficiency but does not provide a memory bound by itself.

The Cornell method and the outline method differ in page structure and main uses.

The Cornell method divides a page into three areas. The note area is on the right. The cue column is on the left. The summary area is at the bottom. You write notes in the note area during a lecture or when you read a text. Later, you write questions or key terms in the cue column. You write a short summary in the bottom area.

The outline method uses indentation and numbering to show the hierarchy of the material. Main topics start at the left margin. Subtopics are indented under each main topic. Supporting details are indented further.

The two methods support different study tasks.

The Cornell method supports these tasks better:
- Recall practice: you can cover the note area and answer the cue questions.
- Self-test: the cue column becomes a quiz when you fold the page.
- Summary: the summary area forces a condensed version of the content.
- Exam review: you can review only the cues before a test.

The outline method supports these tasks better:
- Hierarchy: the layout shows main ideas and their supports.
- Dense lectures: the indent levels separate general points from details.
- Argument structure: the order of headings shows the line of reasoning.
- Missing information: a gap in the indent structure shows that a detail is missing.

The outline method often requires less time during a lecture because you only indent. You can choose the Cornell method when you plan to test yourself later. You can choose the outline method when the material has a clear hierarchy. This choice depends on the content and on your preference.

- Item name and description
- Category (for example, jewelry, electronics, furniture)
- Quantity

Benign overfitting occurs when a model achieves zero training error and still predicts new data well. This behavior appears often in overparameterized models. The term contrasts with the usual view that interpolation causes poor generalization.

Current theory shows that benign overfitting can happen under several conditions. The first condition is a large number of parameters relative to the number of examples. This allows many solutions that interpolate the training data. The second condition is low intrinsic dimension of the data. The third condition is an implicit bias in the training algorithm that selects smooth or low-norm solutions.

The fourth condition is a favorable covariance spectrum for the features. The fifth condition is a sufficient signal-to-noise ratio. These conditions do not guarantee benign overfitting in every case. They describe settings where it is possible.

Many solutions can interpolate the training data. The training algorithm selects one of them. The inductive bias of the algorithm can make the selected solution generalize well. For example, gradient descent can find a solution with small norm. This bias is a key mechanism in benign overfitting.

The usual bias-variance decomposition predicts a U-shaped test error as model capacity grows. In that view, more capacity reduces bias but increases variance. Benign overfitting does not contradict the decomposition. It shows that variance can depend on the data distribution and the algorithm, not only on capacity.

Capacity measures such as parameter count do not fully predict variance. In high dimensions, variance can decrease after the model begins to interpolate. This pattern is called double descent. Therefore, the bias-variance explanation applies but requires a more careful capacity measure.

In technical documents for mixed-skill readers, the choice between a definition at first occurrence and a glossary has trade-offs.

Definition at first occurrence:
- Advantage: It gives new readers the meaning at the moment that they meet the term.
- Advantage: It keeps the explanation local to the text.
- Disadvantage: It can interrupt readers who already know the term.
- Disadvantage: It can make the first sentence longer and less direct.

Glossary:
- Advantage: It keeps the main text short.
- Advantage: It provides one consistent definition for the whole document.
- Disadvantage: It forces readers to move away from the text to find the meaning.
- Disadvantage: Some readers do not look up terms, so they miss the meaning.

You can phrase an inline definition as a short parenthetical phrase after the term. A common form uses only one key attribute and the category, for example, a timeout value (the time that a client waits for a response). Experienced readers can skip the parenthetical phrase and still follow the sentence. The definition does not restate the term. A short phrase uses fewer than 15 words. If a term needs more detail, the glossary can hold that detail and the inline definition can stay very brief.

Leafy greens wilt in dry air. Berries grow mold in humid air. A single drawer with one humidity control cannot provide two humidity levels at the same time.

Conditions to check
- Temperature: The refrigerator temperature must be between 34°F and 40°F (1°C and 4°C).
- Humidity: Leafy greens need high humidity. Berries need low humidity.
- Airflow: The high humidity control closes the air vent. The low humidity control opens the air vent.
- Ethylene: Some fruits release ethylene gas. Ethylene can damage leafy greens.
- Cleanliness: Spoiled produce can spread mold to other produce.
- Packaging: Wet berries grow mold quickly. Dry leafy greens keep longer.

How to adjust
1. Check and set the refrigerator temperature between 34°F and 40°F (1°C and 4°C).
2. Do not store leafy greens and berries in the same drawer.
3. Use two drawers if your refrigerator has them.
4. Set the leafy greens drawer to high humidity.
5. Set the berries drawer to low humidity.
6. Remove damaged leaves and moldy berries.
7. If you wash leafy greens, dry them completely before storage. Store them in a perforated plastic bag or in a container with a paper towel.
8. Store berries unwashed in the original ventilated container or in a container lined with a paper towel.
9. If you have only one drawer, choose low humidity for berries. Store leafy greens in a sealed container on a different shelf.
10. If berries show mold later, discard those berries. Do not eat moldy berries.
11. Check the drawers weekly. Remove spoiled produce immediately.

A tank water heater stores hot water in an insulated tank.
A thermostat keeps the water at a set temperature.
The burner or electric element cycles to maintain that temperature.
A tankless water heater has no storage tank.
It heats water only when a hot water fixture opens.
A flow sensor starts the heat source, and cold water gains heat as it passes through the heat exchanger.

A tank water heater usually has a lower equipment cost and a simpler installation.
A tankless water heater typically costs more to purchase and install.
Installation of a tankless unit often needs a larger gas line, a new vent, or dedicated electrical circuits.
The requirements depend on the home infrastructure.
The first cost of a tankless unit is often higher than the first cost of a tank unit.

A tank water heater needs a periodic flush to remove sediment.
The anode rod in a tank unit also needs inspection and replacement over time.
Sediment and hard water affect the service life of a tank unit.
A tankless water heater has no anode rod.
In hard water areas, a tankless unit needs periodic removal of mineral scale.
Some manufacturers set the interval for scale removal based on water hardness.

A tank water heater loses heat through the tank wall.
This standby loss continues even when no hot water is in use.
A tankless water heater has no standby loss because it stores no water.
The energy use difference depends on the amount of hot water that the household uses.
Large hot water use can reduce the benefit from a tankless unit.
High-efficiency models of either type can lower energy use.

A tank water heater is a better fit for households with high simultaneous hot water demand.
A tankless unit cannot always supply enough hot water for multiple showers and appliances at the same time.
A tankless water heater is a better fit for homes with low hot water use or limited space.
A tankless unit can also be a better fit when long service life matters.
A tank unit is often a better fit when the gas line or electrical panel cannot support a tankless unit.
The best choice depends on hot water use, space, fuel type, and installation limits.

Use these steps to diagnose and fix outline-level structural problems.

1. List all top-level sections in the current outline.
2. Write one sentence that states each section's main claim.
3. Check each main claim against the report's thesis.
4. If a claim does not support the thesis, mark that section for removal or relocation.
5. For each section, list its evidence items.
6. Check each evidence item against the section's main claim.
7. If evidence supports a different section, move that evidence to the correct section.
8. Draw a graph of cross-references between sections.
9. Find cycles in the graph.
10. For each cycle, identify the shared material that two sections need.
11. Move that shared material to an earlier common section.
12. If you cannot move the material, add a forward reference with no backward dependency.
13. If one section's claim depends on another section's claim, nest the first under the second.
14. Repeat the checks after each fix until all pass.
15. Check that each top-level section remains parallel.

Cursor-based pagination uses the last returned row value as a bookmark. It avoids offset drift in changing data. This pattern is common for feeds. It does not give perfect snapshot semantics when rows change between requests. Exact behavior depends on your database isolation level and schema.

Steps
1. Select a monotonic column, for example an auto-increment identifier or a database sequence, for the primary order.
2. Add a unique tie-breaker column, for example the primary key, to make the order total.
3. Create a database index on the order columns and the tie-breaker column.
4. Define the cursor as the encoded values of the last row that the client received.
5. For the first page, run the query with the given limit and no cursor.
6. For subsequent pages, add a WHERE condition that requests rows after the cursor tuple.
7. Use tuple comparison in SQL to preserve index order.
8. Return the next cursor only when you return a full page.
9. Return a null cursor or a flag when no rows remain.
10. Encode the cursor with base64url and include its version to prevent parsing errors.
11. Validate the cursor type and the number of fields before you use it.
12. If the cursor is invalid, return a client error with a clear message.
13. Test the pagination with deleted rows and rows inserted between pages.

Cursor design
The sort key is a monotonic database sequence, for example an auto-increment identifier. New rows have larger sort keys than the current cursor. If the sort key is not unique, a unique secondary key is required. The pair forms a total order. Tuple comparison applies this order. A composite database index supports the query.

The cursor stores the last seen key values, not row references. Deleting the corresponding row does not break the next page request. The query uses a greater-than condition on the cursor tuple. With a monotonic sort key, newly inserted rows appear on later pages without skipping. Rows inserted before the current cursor position require a snapshot to be included. This behavior is standard for append-heavy feeds, and it does not promise a perfect snapshot.

The cursor is a versioned base64url-encoded object. It includes the sort key and the tie-breaker value. It does not expose database row identifiers alone. A typical SQL query uses WHERE (order_col, id_col) > (cursor_key, cursor_id) ORDER BY order_col, id_col LIMIT page_size. This pattern prevents duplicate rows when the client follows the given cursor.

The claim that tutors must match explanations to a student's preferred sensory style is a misconception.

Controlled studies show no reliable benefit that depends on this match. People can prefer one format, but that preference does not predict better outcomes in that format.

Research on tutoring indicates that these mechanisms matter most:

- Feedback that corrects errors and tells the student why the error occurred.
- Prompts for the student to explain the reasoning in his or her own words.
- Scaffolding that adjusts the level of help to the student's current knowledge.
- Guided practice that decreases support as the student improves.
- Clear explanations and work examples that target the student's misconceptions.

Effective tutors first diagnose what the student knows and does not know. Then they give focused help. They ask the student to explain. They give immediate and specific feedback. They withdraw support as the student gains skill.

A match between the explanation's sensory mode and the student's stated preference is not among these reliable mechanisms.

Engineering Stress and Engineering Strain

A tensile test pulls a sample until it breaks. Stress measures force per area. Strain measures length change.

Engineering stress equals the applied force divided by the original cross-sectional area of the sample. Engineering strain equals the change in length divided by the original length. These values use the sample dimensions from before the test. Test reports usually list engineering stress and engineering strain.

True Stress and True Strain

During a tensile test, the sample becomes longer and thinner, so the true area at any moment is smaller than the original area. True stress equals the force divided by the actual area at that moment. True strain equals the total of all small length changes, each divided by the length at that time. A simple formula for uniform deformation is true strain equals the natural logarithm of the final length divided by the original length. The two definitions give almost the same results for very small strains. The difference becomes large when the sample deforms a lot.

When Each Convention Is Used

Engineering stress and engineering strain are standard in routine test reports. Designers use them for elastic analysis and for comparisons with material specifications. True stress and true strain are useful for applications with large deformation. Examples include metal forming and crash analysis. Engineers convert engineering values to true values only up to the point of necking. After necking, the cross-section is not uniform, so direct measurement is required.

CLIMB MILLING AND CONVENTIONAL MILLING

All statements below assume that the machine, the tooling, and the material are used within the manufacturer limits.

MECHANICS
In climb milling, the cutter rotation and the feed direction match at the cutting edge. Each tooth enters at maximum chip thickness and exits at zero thickness. In conventional milling, the cutter rotation opposes the feed direction at the cutting edge. Each tooth enters at zero chip thickness, rubs, and exits at maximum thickness. The difference in chip formation changes the force direction and the result.

TRADE-OFFS

Cutting force and workholding
Conventional milling tends to lift the workpiece from the table. The fixture must resist this lift. Climb milling tends to press the workpiece toward the table. This downward force can assist the clamping. However, the horizontal force in climb milling pulls the workpiece in the feed direction. The workholding must resist this pull.

Backlash
Conventional milling is tolerant of axis backlash because the feed force pushes against the lead screw. Climb milling can pull the table ahead in the feed direction if backlash exists. The table can jump and the cutter can break. Climb milling is safe only on a machine with preloaded ball screws or backlash below the builder limit.

Tool deflection
In conventional milling, the cutter deflects under a force that grows as the chip thickens. The initial rub can cause vibration and poor finish. In climb milling, the cutter deflects away from the cut at the thick entry. The exit at zero thickness produces less tearing.

Surface finish
Climb milling usually gives a better surface finish. The tooth exits with no chip load, so it does not tear the surface. Conventional milling can leave rub marks and recut chips.

Chip evacuation and heat
Climb milling throws chips behind the cutter. This keeps the cut path clear. Conventional milling can carry chips in front of the cutter. These chips can be recut. The initial rub in conventional milling makes extra heat. Climb milling sends more heat into the thick chip, and this can keep the tool cooler.

Machine rigidity
Climb milling needs a rigid spindle, toolholder, and machine structure. Chatter can start if any part flexes. Conventional milling is less sensitive to limited rigidity.

ROUGHING AND FINISHING

For roughing, conventional milling is conservative when the machine has backlash or the workholding is not rigid. Climb milling for roughing is appropriate when the machine has low backlash and the setup is rigid. Climb roughing can remove more material per tooth and send heat into the chip.

For finishing, climb milling usually gives a better surface finish and a more predictable size. Conventional milling for a light finish cut is acceptable only if backlash prevents climb milling. The finish will be worse.

CONSERVATIVE DECISION FRAMEWORK

1. Check the machine backlash with an indicator. If the backlash is above the builder limit, use conventional milling only.
2. Check the workholding. Clamp the part on all locating faces. Tighten all clamps to the specified torque. Push the part by hand. Check that the part does not move.
3. Check the cutter. Measure the runout at the tool tip. Use the shortest tool that reaches the feature. Tighten the toolholder to the specified torque.
4. Check the coolant or air flow. Point the flow at the cut zone.
5. Make a test cut in a scrap area. Use a lower feed and a shallower depth than the planned cut.
6. Monitor the test cut. Listen for chatter. Watch the table for jumps. Stop the spindle if the tool chatters or the table jumps.
7. If the test cut is stable, increase the feed and depth in small steps. Check the size and surface after each step.
8. Use climb milling for the production finishing cut when the test cut is stable.
9. Use conventional milling for the production roughing cut when any check fails.
10. Do not use climb milling on a manual machine with an unlocked table.

Target tracking scaling keeps a chosen metric near a target value. The autoscaler calculates the required number of instances from current load. It adjusts capacity automatically after a metric alarm stays outside the target for a short period. The response to a sudden spike is moderate because the policy waits for the alarm and then adds instances. It often uses less capacity than step scaling for steady traffic.

Step scaling uses explicit thresholds and fixed capacity changes. You define a rule such as add two instances when CPU exceeds 70 percent. You can configure a large step for high load to counter a sudden spike. This method can react faster if the threshold set is low, but it risks overshoot and oscillation. It gives precise control but requires manual tuning.

Predictive scaling uses a forecast from historical load patterns. It adds capacity before a predicted spike, so response latency is low for recurring spikes. It does not react to a novel sudden spike unless a dynamic policy also exists. It can reserve excess capacity when forecasts overpredict demand, which increases cost.

Trade-offs:
- Cost: Target tracking minimizes waste for steady load, but step scaling can add excess capacity with large steps. Predictive scaling can reserve excess capacity when forecasts overpredict demand.
- Response latency: Target tracking has one alarm evaluation delay plus instance launch time. Step scaling has a shorter detection delay if the threshold is low. Predictive scaling eliminates launch delay for predicted spikes.
- Stability: Target tracking dampens oscillations around the target but can still overcorrect during a fast spike. Step scaling can oscillate when thresholds are close. Predictive scaling is stable for known cycles but can mispredict outliers.

Decision:
Target tracking is adequate when traffic changes gradually and cost efficiency is the primary goal. If your sudden spikes are unpredictable and large, a step scaling alarm with an aggressive scale-out rule can respond faster. If your spikes repeat on a daily or weekly pattern, predictive scaling with target tracking as a fallback can reduce latency. The policies can run together. A maximum instance count prevents runaway cost.

Object storage and block storage differ in architecture. Object storage uses a flat namespace and HTTP requests for each object. Block storage exposes raw volumes that the operating system divides into fixed blocks. Applications manage file systems on block volumes. Object storage typically has no file system hierarchy. Block storage requires a file system or database to organize data.

Consistency models differ. Object storage consistency depends on the provider and operation. Amazon S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all object operations in all Regions. Other providers can be eventually consistent for some operations. Block storage gives immediate strong consistency within one attached volume. All reads after a completed write see that write.

Performance characteristics differ. Object storage optimizes for high throughput and parallel access to large objects. Read latency for a specific cold object is often tens of milliseconds. Block storage gives sub-millisecond to low-millisecond latency for random reads and writes. It supports many small random operations per second. Large immutable objects suit object storage, but small mutable records suit block storage.

Cost models differ. Object storage costs less per gigabyte than block storage. You pay for stored capacity and API requests. Block storage charges for provisioned capacity even when unused. Snapshots and replication can add cost. Object storage has no minimum capacity, but block storage often has a minimum volume size.

Access patterns differ. Object storage suits write-once, read-many workloads. Each update rewrites the whole object. This pattern is inefficient for small mutable records. Block storage supports updates to small areas without rewriting the whole volume. Databases and transactional systems use block storage.

A data lake with occasional low-latency reads of specific objects has these trade-offs. Object storage reduces cost for large immutable data. Cold object reads can be slower than required, so you can add a cache layer or a performance tier for hot objects. Block storage gives low latency directly but costs more and scales less. A hybrid design uses object storage for raw lake data and block storage for hot caches. Selection depends on read latency budget and update frequency.

# Guide for Policy Rewrites in Plain Language

## Core Principles

1. Plain language uses short sentences.
2. Plain language puts one idea in each sentence.
3. Plain language uses common words.
4. Plain language uses active voice.
5. Plain language uses the same word for the same meaning.
6. Plain language uses verbs instead of nouns.
7. Plain language states the condition before the result.

## Jargon and Nominalization

Jargon is a word that only some readers know. If the text must keep jargon, the writer defines it the first time. A nominalization is a noun that came from a verb. It hides the action and adds words. Plain language uses the verb instead of the nominalization.

## Before-and-After Examples

These before sentences have jargon and nominalizations. The after sentences are clearer.

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| The committee will make a decision about the request. | The committee will decide about the request. |
| The manager will perform an analysis of the report. | The manager will analyze the report. |
| The utilization of the new procedure will effectuate a reduction in the time to process the request. | The new procedure will reduce the time to process the request. |

Checklists in technical writing are not simple to-do lists. A to-do list identifies actions that a person must complete. A checklist verifies conditions that a document, a procedure, or a review must satisfy. A to-do list supports task completion. A checklist supports quality control. A checklist can be short, but its content defines its function.

The view is mistaken because it confuses task lists with quality control. In complex documentation projects, checklists reduce known types of omission errors. They externalize memory for standards that writers and reviewers must apply to every page. They make review criteria visible and consistent across authors and releases. They also record completed checks and support handoffs between writers and reviewers. That function is a control for known failure modes.

No checklist removes the need for domain knowledge. Its value depends on design, scope, and use. A checklist that repeats common sense items can add overhead without benefit. For large projects, a short, specific checklist often reduces review time and rework.

This comparison applies to deployment pipelines that use a public cloud provider. The trade-offs depend on the provider, the CI/CD platform, and the security policy. User-assigned credentials mean credentials for a human user that the pipeline uses. The three approaches differ in credential lifetime, log attribution, and rotation burden.

**Long-lived keys for a service account**

- Credential management: The team stores the static key in a secret management system. A leak grants long-term access until the team revokes the key.
- Auditability: The logs record the service account as the actor. The logs do not show the pipeline run or the triggering user.
- Rotation: The team must rotate the key on a schedule. If the key expires, a missed rotation causes a pipeline outage.
- Appropriate when: The cloud provider or legacy application does not support workload identity federation. This method is the fallback for such environments.

**Short-lived workload identity federation**

- Credential management: The pipeline does not store long-lived credentials. The identity provider issues a short-lived token for each run.
- Auditability: The identity provider records each token exchange. The logs link the token to a pipeline, repository, and branch.
- Rotation: No static credential exists, so credential rotation is not required. The team manages the trust relationship in the identity provider and in the cloud.
- Appropriate when: The cloud provider and the CI/CD platform support OpenID Connect (OIDC) or a similar protocol. This method is appropriate for new pipelines.

**User-assigned credentials**

- Credential management: The pipeline stores a long-lived password or access key for a human user. A leak gives an attacker the permissions of that user and long-term access.
- Auditability: The logs record the human user as the actor. The logs cannot show whether the person or the pipeline performed the action.
- Rotation: Password changes affect both the user and the pipeline. Uncoordinated rotation causes pipeline failures or account lockouts.
- Appropriate when: Only a temporary bootstrap or a break-glass scenario requires human user credentials. This method is not appropriate for normal deployments.

Likely causes:
- The client uses a low signal threshold and changes only when the signal is unusable.
- The AP cells overlap too little, so the client cannot find a better AP before the current link fails.
- The network does not use 802.11k, 802.11v, or 802.11r. The client gets no neighbor data and then performs a full authentication exchange.
- The AP transmit powers are not balanced. One AP appears stronger than a closer AP.

Trade-offs

RSSI threshold tuning:
A higher threshold makes clients change APs earlier. It can cause frequent changes between APs when the signal is near the threshold. A lower threshold keeps clients on the current AP longer and can cause the observed drop. A controller-side minimum RSSI forces a disconnection at that level. This disconnection can cause an outage if the client sees no better AP or immediately reconnects to the same AP. Manual tuning must account for client-specific signal reporting, and validation in a small area prevents frequent AP changes.

802.11k/v/r support:
802.11k provides neighbor reports and reduces scan time. 802.11v can send a BSS transition management request. This request can steer a client to a better AP before the link fails. These protocols do not force a client to change APs. The client still uses its own threshold. Some clients ignore these requests or implement them incorrectly.
802.11r provides fast transition and reduces authentication time after the decision to change APs. It does not prevent sticky clients. It requires the same mobility domain on all APs and support in the client. The use of 802.11k and 802.11v adds management frames to the airtime. Some older clients process these frames incorrectly. The use of 802.11r reduces the brief outage when a client changes APs, but it does not cause an earlier change.

AP placement adjustments:
AP placement changes the cell overlap and the signal level at the cell edge. Good placement supplies a stronger candidate signal before the current link fails. It can reduce the need for client-specific settings. More APs can improve signal but can increase co-channel interference when the channel set is limited. Lower transmit power on an AP shrinks the cell and can force earlier AP changes. It can also create coverage holes.
Placement changes require a new site survey, cabling, and possible downtime. They improve the physical layer and do not depend on client support. This method has a higher cost than a software change.

No single adjustment fixes sticky clients on all device types. A combination of RSSI threshold tuning, 802.11k/v/r support, and measured AP placement gives the best result.

Do not run this procedure in production first. A wrong timeout can cause false failure detections. Use a test environment.

1. Record the current membership configuration and a rollback plan.
2. Set the gossip fanout to three peers per node.
3. Set the gossip interval to a fixed value with a random jitter of plus or minus ten percent.
4. Coalesce all membership changes that occur within one gossip interval into one message.
5. Send a digest of the membership list in each gossip message.
6. Send the full membership list only when a node joins or a partition heals.
7. Use version vectors to merge membership lists after a partition heals.
8. Do not mark a node failed when it misses one gossip message.
9. Require confirmation from two other nodes before you mark a node failed.
10. Use an indirect probe on a suspect node before failure declaration.
11. Set the failure timeout to a value greater than the maximum expected network delay plus three gossip intervals.
12. If the message rate exceeds the bound, reduce the fanout or increase the interval.
13. If false failure detections exceed the limit, increase the failure timeout.
14. Run a test with simulated partitions and churn.
15. If the test fails, roll back to the recorded configuration.

Coral reef ecosystems and boreal forest ecosystems both have alternative stable states. A coral reef can exist as a coral-dominated state or an algae-dominated state. A boreal forest can exist as a conifer-dominated forest or a shrub, grassland, or wetland state. These states persist because of positive feedback loops.

In a coral reef, a positive feedback loop maintains the coral state. Coral growth creates hard substrate and shelter for herbivorous fish. Herbivorous fish remove algae and open space for coral larvae. If sea temperature rises beyond a threshold, corals expel their symbiotic algae. Scientists call this event coral bleaching. Coral mortality reduces structure and herbivore habitat. Some macroalgae then overgrow the bare substrate and inhibit coral settlement. This feedback can shift the reef past a tipping point. Recovery is slow because the algae state blocks sites for coral recruitment and can persist after the stress ends. Local stressors such as nutrient runoff and overfishing strengthen this loop.

In a boreal forest, fire is a recurring disturbance. Conifer species recover after fire through serotinous cones or vegetative regrowth. A positive feedback loop maintains the forest when fires occur at natural intervals. Forest cover shades the soil and keeps permafrost cold. If fire frequency increases, young trees cannot produce seed before the next fire. The loss of the organic soil layer exposes permafrost to thaw. Thaw changes soil moisture. In low areas, thaw creates waterlogged conditions that prevent conifer regeneration. The system can shift to a shrub or grassland state. That state supports more frequent fire and prevents tree seedling establishment. Recovery is slow or blocked because seed sources become distant and soil conditions change.

The two systems differ in their main triggers. Coral reefs respond mostly to heat stress and water quality changes. Boreal forests respond mostly to fire, temperature, and insect outbreaks. Coral reefs show strong hysteresis because the algae state maintains itself through dense growth. Boreal forests can also show hysteresis after permafrost thaw or the loss of seed sources. In both systems, the original state persists while internal feedback loops are intact. A disturbance must be severe or repeated enough to break those loops. Recovery trajectories depend on whether the alternative state persists without the original stress. Management can support recovery by protecting herbivores on reefs and by controlling fire intervals in boreal forests.

The Nile flood rose and fell at a predictable time each summer. The Tigris and Euphrates floods came at varied times in spring from snowmelt and rain. Their floods were often sudden and destructive. The Nile carried fertile silt and deposited it on the fields. The Tigris and Euphrates also carried salt.

In the ancient period, the Nile valley typically supported a denser and more continuous ribbon of settlement than the Tigris-Euphrates plain. Farmers in Egypt used basin irrigation with short canals and earthen banks. They released stored floodwater after the silt settled. In Mesopotamia, managers built permanent canals, levees, and drainage channels. They maintained these works continuously to control water and to remove salt. The irregular floods required more centralized labor and repair than the predictable Nile flood.

For IPv4, a subnet mask marks the network portion with contiguous 1 bits and the host portion with 0 bits. CIDR notation shows this split as a prefix length after a slash. A /24 prefix uses the first 24 bits for the network and the last 8 bits for hosts. A /23 prefix uses 23 network bits and 9 host bits. The total host address count is 2 to the power of the host bit count. Subtract two addresses for the network address and the broadcast address to get the usable count.

A /24 subnet has 254 usable host addresses. For about 200 devices, this leaves 54 spare addresses before any reservations. A /23 subnet has 510 usable host addresses. A /24 is sufficient if the count will stay below about 250 devices. A /23 is appropriate if future growth is likely. Larger than /23 gives more addresses but you rarely need it for this size.

All hosts in a subnet share one broadcast domain. A /24 has a smaller broadcast domain than a /23. A /23 produces more broadcast traffic because it contains more hosts. Larger subnets increase broadcast traffic and can reduce performance if many devices use broadcast protocols. For 200 devices, both /24 and /23 have acceptable broadcast domain sizes. If the network uses mostly unicast traffic, the broadcast size has little effect.

A /24 supports a maximum of 254 hosts. If the office grows beyond that, you must renumber or use additional subnets. A /23 supports up to 510 hosts and gives more headroom. The trade-off is a larger broadcast domain. For an office with roughly 200 devices now, /23 is common when moderate growth is expected. /24 is common when the count is stable and you want the smaller broadcast domain.

## Likely causes

### Missing VLAN tags

When the NIC has VLAN hardware offload enabled, the driver removes the 802.1Q tag before the frame reaches the kernel. The kernel stores the VLAN ID in packet metadata. A packet capture on the physical interface reads the frame data after tag removal. The capture then shows no VLAN tag.

### Duplicate frames

A duplicate frame has two main causes.

- The capture uses the `any` pseudo-device. The kernel delivers the same frame once on the physical device and once on the VLAN subinterface. This behavior is expected.
- Some network drivers deliver the same frame twice from the receive ring when VLAN offload is active. This behavior is specific to the driver and the NIC.

## Capture approaches that preserve tags without duplication

1. Bind the capture tool to the physical interface only. Do not use the `any` pseudo-device.
2. Disable VLAN tag removal in hardware on that interface with this command: `ethtool -K <physical-interface> rx-vlan-offload off`. On older kernels, use `ethtool -K <physical-interface> rxvlan off`.
3. Confirm the setting with this command: `ethtool -k <physical-interface> | grep rx-vlan`.
4. Capture the traffic with this command: `tcpdump -i <physical-interface> -Q in -e`. The `-e` option shows the link-level header, which includes the VLAN tag when the frame has one.

If you disable rx-vlan-offload, the receive performance for VLAN traffic can decrease. Enable the setting again if performance is more important than tag visibility.

The monsoon system reverses wind direction twice each year. The northeast monsoon blows from November to March. The southwest monsoon blows from June to September. The exact dates vary by latitude and by region. These winds gave pre-steam ships in the Indian Ocean a predictable pattern for long voyages. Ships used the southwest monsoon for voyages to India and the northeast monsoon for return voyages.

Square-rigged ships performed poorly against the wind. Captains planned departures to match the monsoon onset. A late departure meant a long delay. Ports at the points between wind belts became places to wait. Traders unloaded cargo in these ports and waited for the next wind reversal. This process formed a hierarchy of emporia, because ports with safe anchorages and inland routes gained more traffic.

The inter-monsoon doldrums brought light and variable winds. These calms occurred near the equator during the transition months. A ship that entered the doldrums lost steerage way. The crew waited for wind, and sometimes the wait lasted for weeks. This risk forced ships to time their departure carefully. Ports near the doldrum belt offered refuge for ships that arrived too late.

Metrics

Precision is the fraction of predicted high-priority tickets that are truly high priority.
Recall is the fraction of true high-priority tickets that the model flags.
A lower threshold increases recall and decreases precision.
A higher threshold does the opposite.
A false negative is a high-priority ticket that the model misses.
A false positive is a normal ticket that the model marks as high priority.

Procedure

1. Collect a validation set that contains true labels for the high-priority class.
2. Generate predicted probabilities for each example in the validation set.
3. List candidate thresholds from 0.0 to 1.0 in steps of 0.05.
4. For each threshold, mark an example as high priority if its probability is at or above the threshold.
5. Compute precision and recall for each threshold on the validation set.
6. Plot precision and recall for each threshold. This plot is the precision-recall curve.
7. Set the minimum recall that the business accepts for high-priority tickets. Base this value on the cost of a missed ticket.
8. If you know the two costs, compute expected cost for each threshold. Use this formula: (false negatives × cost per false negative) + (false positives × cost per false positive).
9. If no threshold meets the minimum recall, do not deploy the model. Improve the model or collect more data. Then return to step 1.
10. Choose the threshold with the highest precision that also meets the minimum recall. If you computed expected cost, choose the threshold with the lowest expected cost.
11. Check the chosen threshold on a held-out test set. If the recall on the test set is below the minimum, do not deploy the model. Improve the model or collect more data.
12. Document the threshold, the expected recall, and the expected false alarm rate.

The comparison applies to the standard Java runtime and the standard .NET runtime. Java generics use type erasure. C# generics use reified types. The main differences are in runtime type checks, overload resolution, and primitive specialization.

Runtime type checks:
- In Java, a List<String> and a List<Integer> have the same runtime class. You cannot use instanceof with a parameterized type, except for an unbounded wildcard. A cast to a parameterized type does not check the type argument. A later element access can throw ClassCastException.
- Arrays in Java are reified. An array store of an incompatible element throws ArrayStoreException. You cannot create an array of a generic type, for example new List<String>[10].
- Reflection in Java can report declared generic type parameters on fields and methods. It cannot report the type arguments of an object.
- In C#, the runtime keeps each type argument. You can test an object with the expression x is List<string>. This test checks the type argument. A covariant type can match a compatible argument.

Overload resolution:
- In Java, you cannot declare two overloads whose erasure is the same. For example, print(List<String>) and print(List<Integer>) cause a name clash. The compiler generates bridge methods for generic inheritance. These bridge methods can appear in stack traces.
- In C#, List<int> and List<string> are distinct types. You can overload on them. Normal overload resolution is compile-time. For dynamic arguments, the runtime binder uses the actual generic type.

Primitive specialization:
- Java does not allow primitive type arguments. You must use wrapper classes, for example Integer for int. This uses wrapper objects and automatic conversions. Edge cases include null values and performance cost.
- C# allows primitive type arguments, for example List<int>. The runtime generates specialized code for each value type. Storage and access use primitive values directly. There is no wrapper object. Static fields are separate for each constructed generic type in C#. In Java, static fields are shared because the class is the same after erasure.

Serverless platforms enforce a maximum execution time for a function invocation. When a function reaches this limit, the platform stops the invocation and reports a timeout error. The exact timeout limit depends on the cloud platform and configuration. The platform can retry the invocation based on the invocation type and configuration. For asynchronous invocations, the platform typically retries the timed-out function automatically. For synchronous invocations, the caller or an integration service decides whether to retry.

A timeout does not guarantee that the function performed no work. The function can complete side effects before the timeout. The platform stops the container or process at the deadline. External calls can succeed before that deadline. A retry then repeats the work from the start. This repetition can produce duplicate records, duplicate messages, or inconsistent data.

Idempotency makes retries safe. An idempotent function returns the same result and applies the same side effects only once for the same event. To achieve idempotency, the function must use a unique identifier from the event as an idempotency key. The function must store the key with the first successful result or a marker. On a retry, the function must check the key before it repeats side effects. Timeouts make this check critical because the first attempt often fails after side effects complete.

Long-duration workloads require decomposition. The operator must split the work into smaller units that each fit within the limit. Each unit can run as a separate function invocation. A queue or an event stream can distribute the units. For workflows that require coordination, the operator can use an orchestration service such as AWS Step Functions, Azure Durable Functions, or Google Cloud Workflows. These services persist state between steps and manage retries.

Frequent timeouts signal a mismatch between function duration and platform limit. Four options exist. The first option is a longer timeout. The second option is function optimization. The third option is work division. The fourth option is a different compute model such as a container or virtual machine service.

A longer timeout can reduce retries but can increase cost and latency for callers. Function optimization keeps the existing architecture but requires careful performance work. Work division improves resilience but adds complexity around orchestration and state management. A container or virtual machine service removes the timeout limit but adds operational overhead.

The coefficient of performance (COP) is the useful heat transferred divided by the work input. For an ideal Carnot refrigeration cycle, the maximum COP equals the evaporator absolute temperature divided by the temperature lift. For an ideal Carnot heat pump cycle, the maximum COP equals the condenser absolute temperature divided by the same temperature lift. The temperature lift is the condenser saturation temperature minus the evaporator saturation temperature. A larger temperature lift increases the denominator. The ideal limit for the COP therefore decreases.

In a real vapor-compression system, the same trend holds. The compressor must raise the refrigerant pressure from the evaporator pressure to the condenser pressure. A larger temperature lift requires a larger pressure ratio. The compressor work per unit mass increases. The refrigeration effect per unit mass does not increase enough to offset the extra compressor work. The ratio of the heat absorbed to the work input becomes smaller.

To reduce the temperature lift, you can raise the evaporator temperature or lower the condenser temperature. This change requires smaller temperature differences in both heat exchangers. You can get these smaller differences with larger heat transfer areas, better surfaces, or more airflow. The equipment becomes larger and more expensive, and fans or pumps can use more power. A higher evaporator temperature removes less moisture from air and can make the cooled space too warm. A lower condenser temperature can reduce capacity when the heat sink is hot.

This comparison applies to a small team that releases software each week.

| Aspect | Trunk-based development | Short-lived feature-branch workflow |
|---|---|---|
| Integration overhead | Developers merge small changes at least once per day. This keeps integration overhead low. If a team waits several days between merges, merge conflicts increase. | Each feature lives on a branch for one to five days. Merge conflicts grow with branch age and the number of concurrent branches. Integration overhead increases when many branches change the same files. |
| Risk of broken builds | Every merge can break the build. Automated tests and a fast build reduce this risk. Direct commits to the trunk make a broken trunk visible quickly when the team uses continuous integration. The team must stop and fix the trunk before new work continues. | Unfinished work stays on the branch. The trunk stays stable more often. A merge of a long-lived branch can cause unexpected failures. This risk increases with branch age and with large changes. |
| Release flexibility | The trunk stays in a releasable state. Incomplete features stay hidden behind feature flags. The team can release any commit that passes all checks. This approach gives high release flexibility. | A feature enters the trunk only after a review and a merge. The weekly release contains only merged branches. If a feature is incomplete, the team must wait for the next weekly release. This approach gives less release flexibility. |

Servers in distributed systems keep their clocks roughly aligned with the Network Time Protocol (NTP). A remote server cannot trust a single central clock because network messages have variable delay. The client sees the central clock's value from an unknown time in the past. The central clock can fail or become unavailable. The central clock itself can be wrong if it has no external reference.

NTP aims to align server clocks with Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Clock skew is the difference between two clocks at one instant. Clock drift is the rate at which a clock gains or loses time. The offset is the estimated difference between the local clock and a reference clock.

A reference clock is a source of true time, such as an atomic clock or a GPS receiver. Stratum is the distance from a reference clock in the NTP hierarchy. A stratum 1 server connects directly to a reference clock. Round-trip delay is the total time for a request and its reply.

The NTP client does not use one server. It queries several servers and compares their answers. The procedure has these stages:
1. The client selects several servers from different network paths.
2. The client sends a request packet to each server and records the time when it sent the request.
3. Each server replies with its own current time and the time when it received the request.
4. The client records the time when it received each reply.
5. The client calculates the round-trip delay and the estimated offset for each server.
6. The client discards outliers and combines the remaining offsets into one correction.
7. The client applies the correction gradually or steps the clock if the offset is large.

If the estimated offset is small, the client slews the clock. The client changes the clock rate slightly until the offset becomes zero. If the offset is larger than 128 milliseconds, the client steps the clock. The client sets the clock to the new time immediately. A backward step can confuse applications that record event order.

The client repeats this exchange at intervals that depend on the stability of the local clock. Over time, the average offset approaches zero. This process keeps the clock skew among servers within a few milliseconds.

1. Save a copy of the report. Use this copy as your rollback point.
2. Make a list of all numbered section headings. Use the heading numbers exactly as they appear.
3. Make a list of all figure captions. Use the figure numbers exactly as they appear.
4. Search the prose for every cross-reference pattern. Write each reference with its location.
