For a field project that needs both vertical chronology and horizontal site layout, these methods are not mutually exclusive. This comparison treats stratigraphic excavation as the removal of deposits in reverse order of formation. It treats open-area excavation as the exposure of a large horizontal area at one time.

Stratigraphic excavation gives precise vertical control. You remove each deposit separately and record its boundaries. This method builds a clear sequence of layers and features. It preserves the relationships between cuts, fills, and surfaces. You sacrifice speed because each context requires separate recording. You also sacrifice horizontal overview because you excavate a smaller area at one time.

Open-area excavation gives broad horizontal control. You expose large areas and see spatial relationships across the site. This method can give the site layout more quickly. It shows the plans of buildings, activity areas, and site organization. You sacrifice fine vertical resolution if you remove thick layers or use arbitrary levels. You can lose thin deposits or subtle interfaces.

For a project that needs both, use open-area excavation with strict stratigraphic control. Record each deposit across the full area before you remove it. This practice gives both layout and chronology, but it is slower than either method alone. If you must choose one priority, stratigraphic excavation gives better vertical chronology. Open-area excavation gives better horizontal layout.

In summary, stratigraphic excavation trades speed for vertical resolution. Open-area excavation trades vertical resolution for horizontal speed, unless you add strict stratigraphic recording.

A message queue decouples the producer from the downstream service. The producer can submit work even when the downstream service is unavailable. The queue stores messages until the consumer is ready. A synchronous call fails immediately if the downstream service is offline. The queue also retries delivery after a failure. This retry behavior can prevent loss of work.

The queue separates the submission of work from the execution of work. The producer does not wait for the downstream response. Multiple consumers can read from the same queue. That parallelism increases throughput. The queue absorbs traffic spikes and prevents overload of the downstream service. This separation lets the system handle more work per unit of time.

A standard queue does not preserve a strict global order of all messages. If the order of some messages matters, a FIFO queue or a partition key preserves that order. Retries and multiple consumers can change the order for independent messages. A queue that enforces strict order usually limits throughput. The application logic must tolerate a different order.

Most message queues provide an at-least-once delivery guarantee. A consumer can receive the same message more than once after a timeout or a crash. The consumer must be idempotent. Idempotent logic prevents duplicate messages from causing incorrect results. You cannot rely on the queue alone to prevent duplicates. Exactly-once delivery needs extra coordination or consumer data checks.

A message queue adds an extra hop between the producer and the consumer. The producer does not receive an immediate result. The total latency includes the time to write the message to the queue and the time for the consumer to read it. Synchronous calls return the result directly after the downstream service finishes. A queue is suitable for work that can tolerate this added delay. If you need a response in milliseconds, a synchronous call is usually better.

What a lockfile is

A lockfile records the exact versions of all dependencies that the package manager resolved. It can also record integrity hashes for some package managers. The lockfile makes builds reproducible because a build uses the same dependency versions on every machine. If you edit the manifest directly, the manifest and the lockfile no longer match. The package manager then reports that the lockfile is out of date.

Procedure to update the lockfile safely

Caution: Do not edit the lockfile manually. Do not delete the lockfile. If you delete it, the package manager resolves all dependencies again, and versions can change.

1. Make a backup copy of the lockfile.
2. Before you continue, verify that the backup copy exists.
3. Read the documentation for your package manager to find the command that updates the lockfile from the manifest.
4. If the package manager has a dry-run mode, run the dry-run command first.
5. Run the command that updates the lockfile from the manifest.
6. Examine the lockfile changes with a diff tool or a version control diff command.
7. If the changes include unwanted downgrades, restore the backup copy of the lockfile.
8. If you restored the backup, adjust the manifest to avoid those versions.
9. If you adjusted the manifest, repeat the procedure from step 3.
10. Verify that the package manager no longer reports the lockfile as out of date.

A nozzle check pattern with absent lines does not always mean permanent damage to the printhead. A defective printhead is only one possible cause.

These conditions can produce the same pattern:

- Dried ink blocks some nozzles. A built-in nozzle clean function can remove this blockage.
- Air bubbles block the flow of ink in the channels. An air-purge or clean function can remove the air.
- Bad electrical contact stops the drive signal to some nozzles. You can remove the cartridges or printhead and install them again.
- A defective printhead also produces absent lines. Replacement is necessary if clean functions and reinstallation do not restore all lines.

Head alignment is not a likely cause of absent lines in a nozzle check. Alignment changes line position and straightness. It does not block the nozzles.

Exact behavior depends on the printer model. On some models, the printhead is part of the ink cartridge. On other models, it is a separate part.

The printer manual sets a safe limit for clean operations. Too many clean operations can fill the waste ink absorber on some printers.

A relational database stores data in tables. Each table has columns and rows. A constraint is a rule that the database applies to every change. If a change would break the rule, the database rejects the change.

Foreign key constraint

You use a foreign key constraint to prevent a row when a required related record is missing. A foreign key is a column in one table. That column refers to a key column in another table. The database permits an insert only if the value matches an existing value in the referenced column. The database also rejects an update that changes the foreign key value to a missing reference.

For example, an orders table has a customer_id column. You set customer_id as a foreign key to the id column of a customers table. The database rejects an insert with a customer_id that has no matching customer. You declare the foreign key column NOT NULL. If the column allows null, the database permits an insert with no value. A null means no reference, so it does not satisfy your requirement.

Check constraint

You use a check constraint to prevent a value outside an allowed range. You define the constraint on the column. The constraint has a condition that each value must satisfy. For example, you set a check constraint that requires quantity to be at least 1 and at most 100. The database rejects an insert or update with a value outside that range. You declare the column NOT NULL if a missing value must also be rejected.

A null value often passes a check constraint. You use NOT NULL to prevent that.

How to use these constraints

You define constraints when you create the table. If you add a constraint later, you first check that all existing rows satisfy it. The database checks constraints on every insert and update. The database does not require the application to enforce them separately. You define the constraints once, and the database enforces them for all data changes.

Constraint syntax differs by database product. You can refer to the documentation for your product.

Inspect the planner inputs in this order.

1. Get the current plan and compare estimates.
Run this command for your query.
```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ...;
```
Compare the estimated rows to the actual rows.

2. Check statistics age and table modifications.
Run this query.
```sql
SELECT relname, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze, n_live_tup, n_mod_since_analyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'table_name';
```
If n_mod_since_analyze is not zero, run ANALYZE table_name.

3. Inspect column statistics for skew.
Run this query for the filter column.
```sql
SELECT attname, null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds, correlation
FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'table_name' AND attname = 'column_name';
```
Check the frequency of the queried value in most_common_freqs.
If the value is not in most_common_vals, inspect the histogram_bounds array.

4. Inspect cost parameters.
Run these commands.
```sql
SHOW seq_page_cost;
SHOW random_page_cost;
SHOW cpu_tuple_cost;
SHOW cpu_index_tuple_cost;
SHOW effective_cache_size;
SHOW default_statistics_target;
```
A high random_page_cost makes index scans look costly.

5. Check the actual row count for the filter value.
Run this query.
```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM table_name WHERE column_name = 'value';
```
Compare this count to the planner estimate in step 1.

6. If the actual count exceeds the estimate, increase statistics.
Run these commands in a maintenance window.
```sql
ALTER TABLE table_name ALTER COLUMN column_name SET STATISTICS 2000;
ANALYZE table_name;
```
Use a statistics target between 1 and 10000.

7. Test the old index plan in a test session.
Run this command first.
```sql
SET enable_seqscan = off;
```
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the same query.
Compare execution time and buffers between the two plans.

8. Reset the test setting.
Run this command.
```sql
RESET enable_seqscan;
```

Do not change enable_seqscan globally in production. The test setting affects only your session.

A layered architecture organizes a software system into horizontal layers. Each layer has one clear responsibility and talks only to the layer directly below it. A simple web app for online orders has three layers.

The presentation layer shows web pages and receives user input. It sends requests to the business logic layer. It does not contain business rules.

The business logic layer applies the rules of the domain. For example, it checks that a product is in stock. It also calculates the total price of an order.

The data access layer reads data from and writes data to a database. It returns rows to the business logic layer as objects or arrays.

Separation of these layers has these main benefits:
- Developers can change a user interface without changes to business rules.
- Developers can test business rules without a web server or a database.
- Developers can replace the database with a different product and change only the data access layer.

Separation also has these drawbacks:
- A simple change can require edits in three layers.
- The application runs more code for each request, which can reduce performance.
- Developers must keep the boundaries clean or the structure becomes artificial work.

Reference note: safety factors for structural steel connections

This note describes general practice. Exact factors vary by code and edition.

Structural steel codes specify minimum safety factors for connection design. These factors cover normal variation in material strength, fabrication, and load. They also reflect the type of failure. For example, fasteners and welds have more conservative code factors than base metal yield.

Designers add margin when a connection failure is sudden and has no alternative load path. They also add margin when inspection access is poor. This margin accounts for hidden defects, extreme load events, and aging.

Extra margin usually requires more material and stronger fasteners. Weight and cost increase. Robustness improves because the connection can withstand greater hidden damage before failure. The balance depends on the consequence of failure and the planned inspection program.

JSON Patch is a format for a sequence of changes to a JSON document.
RFC 6902 defines the format.
Each operation has an `op` member and a `path` member.
Some operations also have a `value` or `from` member.
The operations run in the order of the array.
RFC 6902 states that a failed operation leaves the target document unchanged.

Operations:
- `add` inserts a value at the path. For an object member that exists, it replaces the value. For an array, it inserts before the given index or at the end when the path ends with `-`.
- `remove` deletes the value at the path. If the path is an array index, the array shifts left.
- `replace` sets the value at the path. The path must exist.
- `move` removes the value from `from` and adds it to `path`.
- `copy` copies the value from `from` to `path`.
- `test` succeeds only if the value at `path` equals `value`. If the values differ, the whole patch fails.

Path syntax:
A `path` uses JSON Pointer syntax from RFC 6901.
A slash starts the path.
Object member names follow the slash.
Array indices appear as zero-based numbers without leading zeros.
The token `-` refers to the end of an array in an `add` operation.
The strings `~0` and `~1` escape the characters `~` and `/`.

When a JSON Patch is better than a full PUT:
A JSON Patch is a better fit when the document is large and the change is small.
A patch sends only the intended changes.
This reduces the risk that it overwrites unrelated fields.
You can include a `test` operation to detect if another client changed a value.
You can use JSON Patch with the HTTP PATCH method for partial updates.
A full PUT replaces the whole resource and can remove fields that the client did not send.

Exact details vary by engine. This answer describes a common implementation. It uses page latches, lock coupling, and internally unique keys for non-unique indexes.

Traversal:
The insert operation starts at the root. The engine searches for the correct leaf page. It acquires a read latch on the root. Then it acquires a read latch on the child that contains the key. It releases the parent latch only after it acquires the child latch. This rule prevents a concurrent split from invalidating the parent pointer.

The engine repeats this process until it reaches the leaf. At the leaf, it upgrades the latch to a write latch. Some engines use a write latch from the start when they detect that a split is possible. The exact choice is version-specific.

Leaf insert and duplicate policy:
When the leaf has free space, the engine inserts the entry. If the key exists, the engine applies the duplicate policy. For a unique index, the insert fails with a duplicate-key error. For a non-unique index, the engine stores the new entry next to existing duplicates. Many engines order duplicate entries by an internal uniqueifier or row pointer.

Leaf split:
If the leaf is full, the engine splits it. It allocates a new leaf page. It moves approximately half of the entries to the new page. The split point is the median entry. The parent stores a copy of the separator key. The full entry remains in the right leaf.

Separator keys in non-unique indexes:
Many engines make non-unique indexes internally unique. They append a row pointer or a uniqueifier to each key. The full key is then (user key, uniqueifier). The separator key is the full composite key of the median entry. This method gives a strict order even when user keys are equal.

Some engines instead store duplicates in an overflow chain. In that design, the leaf split does not separate equal user keys. The separator is the first user key of the new leaf page. If a single duplicate value exceeds one page, the engine must handle the duplicate chain across pages. The method is engine-specific.

The engine inserts the separator key and a pointer to the new leaf into the parent. The old leaf pointer stays in the parent. The engine adds the new pointer after the old pointer. The engine must update the sibling pointer if the tree uses B-link pointers. In a B-link tree, the old leaf points to the new leaf. This pointer lets concurrent readers continue when a split occurs.

Parent split and propagation:
If the parent has free space, the update finishes. If the parent is full, the engine splits the parent. It allocates a new internal node. It moves the second half of keys and child pointers to the new node. The median key moves up to the grandparent. The engine must also set the sibling pointer for the internal node in a B-link tree.

The engine holds write latches on all nodes involved in the split chain. In lock coupling, the engine retains the write latch on the parent until the child split and parent update complete. Then it releases latches from bottom to top.

Root split and tree height:
If the root is full, the engine splits it like an internal node. It allocates a new root. The new root contains one separator key and two child pointers. The old root becomes a child. Tree height increases by one. The root latch remains exclusive for the full operation.

Concurrency correctness:
The lock coupling protocol prevents a concurrent thread from observing a half-updated tree. A thread that searches while a split occurs either sees the old tree before the split or the new tree after the split. In B-link trees, readers do not need to hold latches for long. They follow sibling pointers when a split moves their target key. The engine must set and flush the sibling pointer before it updates the parent pointer. This order is critical for crash consistency.

Parent and child pointer updates during migration:
When a leaf splits, the parent gains a new separator and pointer. The old child pointer remains valid for keys less than the separator. The new child pointer is valid for keys greater than or equal to the separator. In a non-unique index with composite keys, the comparison includes the uniqueifier. The engine updates the parent page in place.

If the parent splits, the grandparent receives a separator and a pointer to the new internal node. The old internal node pointer stays. The engine must also update the right-sibling pointer of the old node to point to the new node. This update happens before the parent update in a B-link tree. Most B-tree implementations do not store parent pointers. If an implementation does store them, the engine must update the parent pointer for every child pointer moved to a new node.

## Trace procedure

1. Identify each response path.
2. Send a request directly to the backend.
3. Record the response headers from the backend.
4. Send the same request through the reverse proxy.
5. Record the response headers from the proxy.
6. Compare the two sets of headers.
7. If a header is present in the direct response but absent through the proxy, check the proxy configuration.
8. If a header is absent in both responses, check the backend framework or server configuration.
9. Run these checks for all missing headers. Use the same method, path, and origin for each test.

## Add headers

10. Add X-Content-Type-Options with the value nosniff.
11. Add X-Frame-Options with the value DENY or SAMEORIGIN. If no page loads in a frame, choose DENY. If the application requires same-origin frames, choose SAMEORIGIN.
12. Add Referrer-Policy with the value strict-origin-when-cross-origin.
13. Add Permissions-Policy. Disable features that the application does not use.
14. Add Content-Security-Policy last. Use a report-only policy.
15. Do not enforce Content-Security-Policy in production first. A strict policy can block pages.
16. Check browser console and report endpoint for violations. Add allowed sources as the application requires.
17. Enforce the policy in staging when no violations occur.
18. Then enforce it in production.
19. If a browser feature breaks, roll back the policy. Change the header to the previous value or remove it.

## Risk evaluation

X-Content-Type-Options with the value nosniff tells the browser to use the declared MIME type. The risk to features is low.

X-Frame-Options blocks framing. DENY blocks all framing. SAMEORIGIN permits only same-origin framing. The risk is low if the application does not use frames.

Referrer-Policy with strict-origin-when-cross-origin sends the origin for cross-origin requests. It sends the full URL for same-origin requests. The risk to features is low.

Permissions-Policy disables browser features that the application does not use. If the application uses a feature, the policy must allow that feature. A policy that disables a used feature breaks that feature.

Content-Security-Policy is the highest risk. A strict policy can block inline scripts, inline styles, images, fonts, media, and connections. The policy requires testing in a staging environment before production use.

The reasoning is not sound.
HTTPS prevents a passive network attacker from reading traffic between the browser and the server. A passive network attacker cannot read traffic between the browser and the server when HTTPS is active. It cannot prevent script execution in the browser. A cross-site scripting (XSS) attack runs JavaScript in the same origin as the app. That script can call window.localStorage.getItem and read the token.

CORS does not block this read because the script is same-origin. The script can then send the token in a form submission, in an image URL, or through fetch with no-cors mode. CORS restricts cross-origin reads, but it does not prevent data transfer to a cross-origin endpoint. A non-browser client is not subject to CORS.

Cookie flags reduce some risk, but they do not make localStorage safe. JavaScript cannot read a cookie that has the HttpOnly flag. Thus an HttpOnly session cookie is not directly stolen by XSS. But if the token is in localStorage, HttpOnly does not apply. SameSite limits when a browser sends a cookie with a cross-site request. It does not stop an XSS script that is already on the origin.

A malicious service worker on the same origin can intercept fetch requests and read an Authorization header that contains a token from localStorage. The worker cannot read the HttpOnly cookie header. It can serve modified responses and cause persistent script execution. A service worker registered on a subdomain cannot intercept requests to the parent origin directly. It can intercept requests to that subdomain and tamper with responses that the parent app consumes.

Subdomain cookie scope adds another risk. A cookie set for example.com is sent to all subdomains of example.com. An XSS on any subdomain can make authenticated requests because the cookie travels with those requests. If that parent-domain cookie lacks HttpOnly, a subdomain XSS can read its value. The same subdomain XSS cannot read localStorage from another origin. localStorage has stronger origin isolation than a parent-domain cookie.

Therefore, do not rely on HTTPS and CORS alone. Use an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie for long-lived session tokens, and apply strict input validation to prevent XSS.

## Procedure to identify the operational risks

1. Define each commitment in measurable terms. State the availability formula, the response start time, and the meaning of fix.
2. Map the service architecture. List each component, external dependency, and deployment path.
3. Review the incident history for the last 12 months. Identify all failures that exceeded the target thresholds.
4. Test the response process from ticket creation to first action. Record the actual time for severity-1 incidents.
5. Examine the fix workflow for severity-2 defects. Identify steps that depend on vendors, customers, or internal approvals.
6. List failure modes outside the provider control. Separate these from controllable risks.
7. For each risk, estimate the probability and the downtime impact. Use data from the incident history and architecture review.
8. Record all risks in a register. Assign an owner to each risk.

## Main operational risks

A 99.9% monthly availability target permits about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month. The exact limit depends on the month length. This calculation assumes a 24/7 measurement. The provider calculates monthly availability as uptime divided by total minutes in the month. The provider either reduces the denominator or adds excluded time to uptime. The contract must state the method.

The main risks for availability are these:

- A single point of failure causes a full outage when that component fails.
- A bad deployment breaks service for all users.
- Insufficient capacity causes overload at traffic peaks.
- An external dependency fails without notice.
- A security incident forces a shutdown.

The main risks for the 4-hour severity-1 response time are these:

- No 24/7 on-call staff causes a delay outside business hours.
- Alert fatigue makes responders ignore critical alerts.
- Unclear severity definitions cause tickets to go to the wrong team.

The main risks for the 10-business-day severity-2 fix window are these:

- A vendor patch that fixes the defect is outside the provider control.
- The defect is hard to reproduce in the test environment.
- The fix requires a large code change and long regression tests.
- The development team lacks enough available capacity.

The term fix is ambiguous. A workaround is not a permanent fix unless the contract states that definition. The response time starts when the customer files a valid ticket through the agreed channel. A mere acknowledgment is not a response. The provider must start diagnosis.

## Procedure to structure exclusions, maintenance windows, and remedies

9. Limit exclusions to events outside the provider control. Include customer misuse, third-party failures, and force majeure.
10. Define planned maintenance windows with advance notice. Set the maximum duration for each window.
11. Exclude only time within approved maintenance windows. Time beyond the window counts against availability.
12. Set a monthly maintenance budget. Example: 4 hours per month.
13. Require emergency maintenance notice. Decide if emergency time is excluded from availability.
14. Define remedies for each missed commitment. Use service credits that scale with the breach.
15. State the credit calculation in the contract. Link repeated breaches to a termination right.

## Enforceability notes

For enforceability, the provider keeps logs of uptime and incident timestamps. The customer receives a monthly report. The customer has the right to audit the logs. The exclusions must not cover the provider's own deployment failures or capacity issues. A common structure credits 5 percent of the monthly fee for each full hour beyond the allowed downtime.

Reference: Evidence for Evolution by Common Descent

Three independent lines of evidence support the theory that all living organisms share common ancestors. These lines are the fossil record, comparative anatomy, and molecular sequence data. Each line has limits for what it can establish about evolutionary rate and mode.

Fossil Record

The fossil record contains a sequence of organisms in rock layers. This sequence shows a consistent order from older to younger layers. Transitional fossils show a mix of traits from two groups. One example is Archaeopteryx, which has feathers and teeth. The stratigraphic position of a fossil gives its relative age. These patterns match the order of lineages that common descent predicts.

The fossil record can establish the relative timing of morphological change. It shows that some lineages have long periods with little change and short periods with rapid change. Scientists name this pattern punctuated equilibrium. For well-sampled lineages with absolute dates, it can give a rate of change in measurable traits.

The fossil record cannot show the genetic changes that caused the morphological changes. It cannot distinguish gradual change from rapid change when rock layers have gaps. Preservation bias prevents a complete record of all transitions. It cannot establish the molecular rate of evolution. It cannot directly show the mode of genetic change at the population level.

Comparative Anatomy

Comparative anatomy finds homologous structures in different species. Homologous structures have the same basic layout but different functions. Examples include the forelimb bones of mammals. Vestigial structures are reduced parts that have no current function. The distribution of shared traits forms a nested hierarchy. This nested hierarchy matches the pattern of common descent.

Comparative anatomy can establish the relative amount of morphological divergence between species. It can show which traits are conserved across long periods. It can suggest a mode of change through structural constraints. It can show that homologous structures result from descent with modification.

Comparative anatomy cannot give absolute dates for divergence. It cannot measure the rate of change per unit time without fossil or molecular data. It cannot show the genetic basis for the observed morphological differences. Similar structures can also arise by convergent evolution. Comparative anatomy cannot always distinguish homology from convergence.

Molecular Sequence Data

Molecular sequence data compare DNA or protein sequences from different species. Shared sequence similarity follows a nested hierarchy. Pseudogenes show mutations that disable function. Endogenous retroviruses occur at the same positions in related genomes. In most sequences that code for proteins, synonymous substitutions accumulate faster than nonsynonymous substitutions. These patterns match the order of lineages that common descent predicts.

Molecular sequence data can establish the relative timing of divergence events with a molecular clock. A molecular clock uses sequence differences and fossil calibration to estimate divergence times. It can measure the rate of sequence change in substitutions per site per year. It can test for natural selection with ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions. It can reveal the mode of change, such as neutral drift or selection, at specific loci.

Molecular sequence data cannot establish a rate without external calibration. Different lineages can have different molecular rates. Horizontal gene transfer and incomplete lineage separation can obscure the tree order. Sequence similarity does not directly show ancestral phenotypes. It cannot show the morphological rate of change without fossil data.

Exactly-once does not mean one copy on the wire. It means that the application sees each business event once. No transport protocol gives exactly-once between independent systems. End-to-end exactly-once requires cooperation from the producer, the broker, and the consumer. Each layer has a different guarantee.

Guarantees at each layer

- Producer to broker: A producer can send a message with a unique ID and wait for an acknowledgement. A broker can reject duplicate IDs from the same producer session. Without idempotence, a retry after a lost acknowledgement creates a duplicate.
- Broker storage: A log-based broker keeps each record at an offset. It does not detect two different IDs that carry the same business event.
- Consumer: A consumer reads each offset in order. It can commit the offset before or after it applies a side effect. The commit order determines the failure mode.

Why duplicates and lost updates happen

Duplicates occur when a producer retries a send after a timeout, but the first send reached the broker. They also occur when two producer instances send the same business event with different IDs. On the consumer side, a duplicate read occurs when a failure happens after a side effect but before an offset commit. A duplicate side effect occurs when the consumer retries a message that an earlier run already applied. A unique ID and an idempotent operation stop this.

Lost updates occur when the consumer commits the offset before the side effect completes. A crash after the commit and before the side effect loses the message. They also occur when a broker retention policy removes a message before the consumer reads it. They occur when a producer drops a message without a retry. These conditions are common causes.

Steps to find the cause

1. Get read access to producer logs, broker logs, consumer logs, and the side-effect database.
2. Add a unique business ID to each message at the producer.
3. Record the business ID and producer timestamp at the source.
4. Enable broker log capture for received messages and offsets.
5. Compare the producer log with the broker log for duplicate IDs.
6. If a duplicate ID appears with two publish attempts, check producer retry settings.
7. If two different IDs carry the same business event, check for two producer instances.
8. On the consumer, record each consumed message ID and its action ID.
9. Store this record in the same database as the side effect, in one transaction.
10. Compare the consumer record with the broker offset log.
11. If the consumer processed an ID more than once, check whether the side effect is idempotent.
12. If an offset advanced without a side effect record, check the commit order.
13. Put poison messages in a dead letter queue and record each one.
14. Before you change retry or commit settings, reproduce the issue in a test environment.

Likely causes

Layer caching

Docker caches each layer by the checksum of its instruction and inputs. A change in an earlier layer invalidates all later layers. If the Dockerfile copies application source files before it installs dependencies, every source change causes a full dependency installation. This increases build time and image size. The instruction order in the Dockerfile therefore affects cache reuse.

Base image choice

Large base images such as Ubuntu include many packages that the application does not use. Each unused package increases the image size and the attack surface. A smaller base image such as Alpine or a distroless image reduces size. A smaller base image can lack debugging tools and common system libraries. A base image that provides only the required runtime reduces unnecessary components. A pinned base image digest makes builds reproducible.

Build context

The build context includes all files in the directory that you pass to the build command. The Docker client sends this context to the daemon. A context with logs, caches, and source archives consumes time and bandwidth. Missing .dockerignore files cause unnecessary files to enter the context. This condition slows local and remote builds.

Trade-offs for reducing image size

Multi-stage builds separate build tools from runtime files. This reduces the final image size and the attack surface. The final stage contains only the binaries and libraries that the application needs. Reproducibility improves when you pin base image digests and dependency versions in each stage. The trade-off is a more complex Dockerfile and longer initial build time.

Smaller base images reduce image size but can introduce compatibility problems with glibc-dependent software and package availability. Application testing on the chosen base image identifies compatibility issues before deployment. The security benefit is a smaller attack surface.

A low layer count with combined RUN commands reduces image size. The trade-off is less cache granularity. A change in one part of a combined command invalidates the whole layer. The placement of stable instructions early and variable instructions late balances cache reuse and size reduction.

Package caches persist if you install dependencies and run cleanup in separate layers. Combining the install and cleanup in one RUN command prevents this persistence. The trade-off is a less readable Dockerfile.

Build layers must not contain secrets. Secrets that appear in a layer persist even after deletion in a later layer. BuildKit secrets or multi-stage builds keep secrets out of the final image. This protects security and reduces image pollution.

Service Mesh Responsibilities in Kubernetes

A service mesh manages service-to-service communication through sidecar proxies. The proxies enforce mutual TLS, traffic split, and retry policies. These features interact with application timeouts and idempotency.

mTLS

The mesh uses certificates to encrypt traffic and to verify peer identity. The handshake and encryption add latency to each request. Application timeouts must include this added latency. If certificate rotation fails, the proxy rejects new connections. The application sees connection failures that look like timeouts.

Traffic Split

The mesh sends a percentage of requests to different service versions. The application cannot assume that one version handles all requests. A retry after an error can go to a different version. That version can have different side effects or data. Non-idempotent operations can execute more than once with different results.

Retries

The mesh can retry a failed request automatically. The application must assume that a request can execute more than once. Non-idempotent operations must have an idempotency key at the application layer. Mesh retries can continue after the application timeout expires. The application can see a timeout while the operation succeeds later.

Edge Cases

The mesh can mask backend failures. A retry that succeeds hides the original error from the application. The mesh can add latency through retries and mTLS overhead. Each retry consumes part of the application timeout budget. If the timeout is too short, the mesh cannot complete enough retries.

A mesh-wide retry policy can retry non-idempotent POST requests. This action causes duplicate writes. Traffic split can route a retry to a different version. That version can have different side effects.

The sidecar proxy adds one network hop. Under load, this hop can exceed the application timeout. mTLS handshake failures can appear as application timeouts. The application cannot distinguish a TLS failure from a slow backend.

They check system-level constraints such as dependency direction, layering, component coupling, and allowed communication paths. These checks prevent architectural drift across many modules.

Unit tests verify behavior inside a module. Static analysis does not check runtime properties such as live dependency graphs, performance under load, or resilience after failures.
