Use this sequence for a leaked credential.

1. Ensure that you have identity provider admin access, repository admin access, and log access.
2. Identify the credential and its permissions from commit history and configuration files.
3. Check the repository visibility, forks, and clones to determine who can see the commit.
4. Revoke the credential in the identity provider immediately.
5. Issue a replacement credential.
6. Update all authorized services to use the replacement credential.
7. Remove the credential from all branches, tags, and commit history in the primary repository.
8. Ask fork owners to remove the credential from their forks.
9. Check that the old credential no longer works in any environment.
10. If the old credential still works, repeat steps 4 through 6.
11. Check access logs for any use of the old credential.
12. Determine the exposure scope from the log data and the credential permissions.
13. Add a secret scanner that blocks known secret patterns in future commits.
14. Require secret storage in a vault or environment variables from this point forward.
15. Document the incident and the fixed process for the team.

Trade-offs

Immediate rotation stops active misuse. It reduces the time that an attacker can use the credential. A log audit after rotation still shows past use of the credential. Immediate rotation can break legitimate services that still use the old credential. You must update those services at the same time.

If the repository is public, assume that the credential is compromised. If you audit logs first, the credential remains valid. An attacker can continue to use it during the audit. The audit can show attacker methods and targets before you remove access. That information can help the investigation.

For most leaked credentials, rotate first. The risk of continued misuse is greater than the benefit of extended observation. If the credential has very high value, you can collect logs for a very short period before rotation. A short delay must be a deliberate decision with an active watch. Do not delay rotation for a credential that grants production access or data access. The exposure continues until you revoke the credential.

Your colleague's view is incomplete. Domain-Driven Design includes strategic design and tactical design. Tactical patterns such as entities, value objects, repositories, and aggregates are one part of DDD. These patterns help you to model a domain in code. They do not define domain boundaries or a shared language.

Strategic design contributes three main things. Ubiquitous language is a shared language that connects code names to business meaning. In a large legacy system, inconsistent terms cause errors and slow changes. Bounded contexts define explicit boundaries around separate models. Each context has its own model and its own language. This separation prevents one large ambiguous model.

Context mapping shows the relationships between bounded contexts. It identifies which team owns each context and how contexts exchange data. In a legacy system, context mapping exposes hidden dependencies. It lets you isolate one context for migration. You can then replace that context without a full rewrite of the system.

Tactical patterns alone do not handle these concerns. They do not tell you where one model ends and another begins. They do not give you a shared vocabulary across teams. Strategic design is not a formal guarantee of success. Its benefits depend on how teams apply the patterns. But in a large legacy system, strategic design often gives more value than tactical patterns alone.

The choice matters beyond noise reduction when the objective has saddle points or ill-conditioned curvature.
Full-batch gradient descent uses the exact gradient at each step.
Stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent use noisy estimates.
For smooth non-convex objectives, full-batch descent has a worst-case rate of O(1/T) for the minimum gradient norm.
Stochastic descent with a step size that decreases has a worst-case rate of O(1/√T).

These rates only guarantee that some gradient becomes small.
They do not guarantee escape from saddle points.
At a saddle point, the exact gradient can be very small.
Deterministic descent can remain in that region for a long time.

The worst-case escape time can be exponential in the dimension.
Stochastic noise can push the iterate away from the saddle.
This effect is not guaranteed.
The noise must project onto a negative curvature direction.
Mini-batch noise has smaller variance than single-example noise.
A large batch can therefore preserve the slow escape behavior of full-batch descent.

Full-batch descent is deterministic.
It converges to a stationary point if the step size is less than one over the Lipschitz constant and the function is smooth.
Stochastic descent with a constant step size does not converge to a point.
It converges only to a neighborhood.
The neighborhood radius grows with the step size and the noise level.

A learning rate schedule that decreases can remove this neighborhood.
The schedule must satisfy two conditions.
The sum of the step sizes must be infinite.
The sum of the squared step sizes must be finite.
If the schedule decays too fast, the iterate can stop before a stationary point.
A small constant step size also slows escape from saddle points because the gradient is already small.

Momentum stores a weighted sum of past gradients.
It moves faster along directions with a consistent gradient sign.
It damps motion along directions that oscillate.
For ill-conditioned quadratic objectives, momentum can improve the convergence rate.
Near a saddle point, momentum can carry the iterate through flat regions.

But momentum can overshoot narrow minima.
The momentum coefficient must be less than 1.
A coefficient close to 1 can cause instability.

Adaptive methods scale each coordinate separately.
They use past gradient magnitudes to adjust the step size per coordinate.
This adjustment can reduce the effect of a large condition number.
On an ill-conditioned Hessian, adaptive methods often move faster than plain gradient descent.
At a saddle point, coordinates with historically small gradients get larger effective steps.
This can speed escape.

This acceleration is not uniform for all non-convex objectives.
Adam with a constant learning rate can fail to converge to a stationary point.
AMSGrad or a decreasing learning rate restores the usual guarantee under standard assumptions.

Standard convergence guarantees fail in these cases:
- The objective lacks Lipschitz continuous gradients.
- A degenerate saddle can trap deterministic methods for a long time.
- The condition number grows with the dimension.
- The gradient noise has unbounded variance or heavy tails.
- The learning rate schedule does not satisfy the two conditions above.
- The momentum coefficient is too high.
- An adaptive method uses a constant learning rate without a correction.
- The function is non-smooth or has discontinuities.
- You evaluate convergence by loss value, not by gradient norm.

A weld is not glue. It joins two metal parts in a controlled way. The heat makes a small area at the edges liquid. That liquid metal cools and becomes solid again. The two edges then share metal across the joint. In this way, the parts become one piece.

Some joints have a gap or need extra metal. A filler material supplies that metal. The filler has a composition that matches the base metal. It melts into the liquid pool and becomes part of the joint. Not all welds use filler. Some methods press the edges together and join them directly.

Hot metal reacts with air. Oxygen and nitrogen can enter the liquid metal. These elements form weak compounds or gas pockets in the joint. A shielding gas flows around the hot area and keeps air away. Common shielding gases are argon, helium, and carbon dioxide. Some methods use a flux instead of a gas.

Enough heat must melt the edges, but extra heat causes problems. The heat-affected zone is the metal next to the weld that gets hot but does not melt. Too much heat makes this zone large. The large zone has weaker mechanical properties than the base metal. It can have large grains, cracks, or lost alloy elements. These changes can make the joint fail under load.

These practices exist to prevent weak joints and failure. A weld without filler or gas can crack under load. Heat control prevents distortion and cracks. Welders use procedures that set the correct current, speed, and gas flow. This control keeps the joint strong and safe.

Technical Note: Coordinate Reference Systems and Datum Transformations

Coordinate Reference Systems

A coordinate reference system (CRS) defines positions on the Earth. A geographic CRS uses latitude and longitude in angular units. A projected CRS uses a map projection to convert latitude and longitude to plane coordinates. Plane coordinates use linear units such as meters or feet. The datum defines the ellipsoid, the origin, the axes, and the orientation. The EPSG registry provides standard codes for CRS definitions.

Geodetic Datums

A geodetic datum connects coordinates to the physical Earth. The datum includes a reference ellipsoid and a set of reference points. The ellipsoid approximates the size and shape of the Earth. The origin and orientation fix the ellipsoid to the Earth. Different datums can have ellipsoids with different positions. Coordinates in one datum do not match coordinates in another datum.

Horizontal Datum Transformations

A datum transformation converts coordinates from one geodetic datum to another. Helmert transformations are common methods. A three-parameter Helmert transformation applies translation only along the X, Y, and Z axes. A seven-parameter Helmert transformation adds rotation and scale. Grid-based transformations use correction grids such as NTv2 or NADCON.

The transformation accuracy depends on the source data and the method. Accuracy varies by location. A grid method is more accurate inside its defined area. The area of use limits the valid domain of a transformation.

Time-Dependent Transformations

Some geodetic datums change over time because of plate tectonics. The International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF) uses an epoch for each realization. Coordinates in ITRF2014 at epoch 2010.0 differ from coordinates at epoch 2020.0. Time-dependent transformations include velocities for each station or a plate motion model. Software must know the coordinate epoch to apply the correct transformation. Static CRS definitions do not capture these changes, but dynamic CRS definitions include the epoch and the velocity model.

Vertical Datums and Transformations

A vertical datum defines the reference surface for heights. Ellipsoidal heights measure from the ellipsoid. Gravity-related heights measure from the geoid or a local vertical datum. The geoid is an equipotential surface that approximates mean sea level. Geoid undulation models convert ellipsoidal heights to orthometric or normal heights.

A compound CRS combines a horizontal CRS and a vertical CRS. Vertical transformations are separate from horizontal transformations. A geoid model provides the undulation value at a location. The software applies the undulation to convert between height types. Ignoring vertical datum differences can cause errors of several meters.

Legacy Data with an Unknown CRS

Legacy data can lack CRS metadata. No reliable automatic method exists to identify an unknown CRS from coordinates alone. Coordinate ranges, units, and spatial extent provide clues. Metadata, map sheets, or known landmarks help to infer the CRS. A temporary CRS assignment requires validation against reference data.

An incorrect datum assignment can cause coordinate shifts of hundreds of meters. The original data must remain unchanged during the test. The assumed CRS and the validation steps require documentation. This workflow prevents accidental modification of the source data.

Common Pitfalls in Projection during Display

- Modern GIS software can reproject layers to a common CRS during display.
- Many GIS packages pick a default transformation if multiple options exist.
- The default transformation can be less accurate than another method.
- Missing grid files can cause an error or a fallback to a less accurate method.
- Reprojection during display can hide an incorrect CRS assignment.
- Axis order differences between CRS definitions can cause swapped coordinates.
- Unit conversion can introduce small errors or hide large ones.
- The software does not always apply the best transformation automatically.
- Large datasets can increase the time for reprojection.

Database normalization is a process that organizes data into separate tables. It reduces duplicate data. It prevents inconsistent data after updates.

The example uses a table named Orders. Its columns are OrderID, CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress, ProductID, ProductName, ProductPrice, Quantity, and OrderDate. Each row stores one product for one order. Customer data repeats for every product in the same order.

This design causes an update anomaly. For example, customer 101 changes address. The address appears in every order row for customer 101. You must update each row. If you miss one row, the table shows two different addresses for the same customer. That is an update anomaly.

Insert and delete anomalies also appear. You cannot add a new product until an order uses that product. If you delete the last order for a customer, you lose that customer's address.

Normalization uses functional dependency. A value determines another value. For example, CustomerID determines CustomerName. ProductID determines ProductPrice. OrderID and ProductID together determine Quantity.

The normalization steps are:

- First normal form requires atomic values. Each cell holds one value. A table with many products per order splits into separate rows.

- Second normal form removes partial dependencies. The composite key is OrderID plus ProductID. OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, and CustomerAddress depend only on OrderID. ProductName and ProductPrice depend only on ProductID. Normalization moves these groups into separate tables. The result is three tables:
   - Orders table: OrderID, CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress, OrderDate
   - Products table: ProductID, ProductName, ProductPrice
   - OrderItems table: OrderID, ProductID, Quantity

- Third normal form removes transitive dependencies. In the Orders table, CustomerID determines CustomerName and CustomerAddress. CustomerID is not a key. Normalization moves those attributes to a Customers table. The final tables are:
   - Customers table: CustomerID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress
   - Orders table: OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate
   - Products table: ProductID, ProductName, ProductPrice
   - OrderItems table: OrderID, ProductID, Quantity

This design removes the update, insert, and delete anomalies for these dependencies.

Third normal form is enough for most transactional systems because it removes redundancy that causes common update anomalies. It is not always necessary because normalization splits data into many tables. Queries then join the tables. Joins can slow the system and add complexity. If the data changes rarely or read speed matters more, you can accept some duplicate data. In rare cases, Boyce-Codd normal form or higher forms are necessary to remove anomalies that third normal form permits.

AWS does not allow a VPC peering connection between VPCs that have overlapping CIDR blocks. The route tables can still contain overlapping destination prefixes from different routes. Each subnet uses one route table. If a subnet has no explicit association, it uses the main route table. The behavior below applies to route tables in a VPC.

Traffic that leaves an instance uses the route table for its subnet. The instance operating system also has its own route table. The VPC route selection starts after the packet leaves the instance. The VPC router does not use instance-specific route tables. The route with the longest prefix match wins for that packet. If no route matches, the VPC drops the packet.

The VPC router uses the longest prefix match. It first selects the route with the longest prefix that matches the destination IP address. For example, a route for 10.0.1.0/24 wins over a route for 10.0.0.0/16 for destination 10.0.1.5. If two routes have the same prefix length and destination, the priority is: local route, then static route, then propagated route.

Each route table has a local route for the VPC CIDR. You cannot delete or change this route. A more specific route can override the local route for a subset of the VPC CIDR. For example, a route for 10.0.1.0/24 to a NAT gateway sends 10.0.1.5 to the NAT gateway. The local route still handles other addresses inside the VPC CIDR.

A prefix list contains multiple CIDR blocks. You can use a prefix list as a route destination. The VPC router treats each CIDR block in the prefix list as a separate route. Longest prefix match applies across prefix list entries and other routes. A prefix list route is a static route. It has priority over a propagated route with the same destination.

A virtual private gateway or a transit gateway can propagate routes from VPN or Direct Connect. You can enable route propagation on the route table. Propagated routes appear in the route table with the target gateway. Longest prefix match applies first. A more specific propagated route wins over a less specific static route. If the destination prefix length is the same, the static route wins.

A route can have blackhole as its target. A blackhole route drops traffic that matches its destination. Blackhole routes take part in longest prefix match. They can block traffic to a specific CIDR even if a less specific route also matches. AWS can create a blackhole route when a route target becomes unavailable.

A Novak-style concept map is a hierarchical graph of concept nodes. Links carry labels that form propositions. A mind map starts from one central node with radial branches. Mind map links usually have no labels. A semantic network is a more general graph of concepts. Its links can be labeled or unlabeled.

Concept maps follow Ausubel's assimilation theory. New knowledge becomes meaningful when a learner links it to relevant prior concepts. A labeled proposition states one unit of meaning. Hierarchies show subsumption from general to specific concepts. Cross-links connect concepts in different branches. Integrative reconciliation occurs when a learner links previously separate concepts.

For advanced learners, cross-links and labeled propositions provide stronger evidence than node recall. A correct labeled link shows that the learner can state a relation between two concepts. A cross-link shows integration across separate parts of the map. Assessors can assess the accuracy and quality of these relations. This assessment is more direct than a multiple-choice test and can indicate deep understanding. However, assessment can require clear rubrics and expert benchmark maps.

Ill-structured domains contain concepts with context-dependent meaning. They often support multiple valid perspectives. Concept maps force a single hierarchy and precise labels. This constraint can distort such domains. Cross-links can proliferate and reduce readability. Expert maps can differ without one correct answer, and this difference lowers assessment reliability.

Therefore, concept maps are most valid in well-structured domains. In ill-structured domains, they can support formative discussion and reflection. High-stakes summative assessment is less reliable in such domains.

## Procedure

Follow these steps in the given order.

1. Split the data into a train set and a holdout test set.
2. Keep the holdout test set untouched until final evaluation.
3. Inspect the train set and record feature types, missing rates, and category counts.
4. Remove identifier columns and any column that contains target information.
5. Merge rare categorical levels in the train set and save the mapping.
6. Use native missing value support in your gradient boosting library if available.
7. If you impute, compute all imputation values from the train fold only.
8. Add a missing indicator column when missingness carries information.
9. Encode low-cardinality categorical features with one-hot encoding.
10. Encode high-cardinality categorical features with cross-validated target encoding and a fallback for unseen categories.
11. Unless the categories have a true order, do not apply ordinal encoding.
12. Do not scale or transform numeric features for skew in a standard gradient boosting tree model.
13. Detect outliers with domain rules and robust quantile bounds from the train set.
14. If you cap or transform outliers, save the parameters before you apply them.
15. Assemble all steps into one reproducible pipeline with fixed random seeds.

## Trade-offs

A split before any data preparation prevents leakage. All statistics must come from the train set.

Full dataset imputation leaks target information. A safe imputation computes statistics from training folds only.

Native missing handling lets the model learn a default direction. Imputation keeps the data complete but can hide informative missingness.

One-hot encoding is safe but creates many sparse columns for high cardinality. Target encoding compresses categories but overfits without out-of-fold estimates, smoothing, and a fallback for unseen categories.

Ordinal encoding imposes false order on unordered categories. It is correct only for ordered levels.

Standard gradient boosting trees do not need feature scaling or skew transforms. Splits compare order. Monotone transforms do not change split quality. Histogram-based bin resolution can change after a monotone transform.

Tree models are robust to outliers because splits use rank order. Extreme values can create isolated splits. Value capping is justified only when domain knowledge supports it.

This order ensures that every transformation is learned from the train data only and is reproducible.

SLSA v1.0 Build Track Summary

This summary covers the Build track of SLSA v1.0. The Source track has separate requirements.

Level 1
- The build process generates provenance. The provenance identifies the artifact, the builder, the top-level source, and the build command. The producer can publish this provenance.
- A consumer can read the provenance but cannot verify that it is authentic.
- Unaddressed threats: An attacker who controls the build process can alter the artifact or the provenance. Dependency changes are not recorded. There is no integrity guarantee.

Level 2
- A hosted build platform generates and signs provenance. The signature binds the provenance to the builder identity.
- The platform records the source revision and build invocation. A consumer verifies the signature and checks that the subject digest matches the artifact.
- Unaddressed threats: A malicious build step can alter the output or fetch a malicious dependency. Platform administrators can tamper with provenance. An attacker in another tenant can influence the build.

Level 3
- A hardened build platform creates non-falsifiable provenance. Builds run in isolated environments. The platform records all build dependencies.
- The platform generates provenance outside the build environment. The build process cannot change the provenance. A consumer verifies the signature, the builder identity, and the complete input list.
- Unaddressed threats: A compromise of the platform control plane can falsify provenance. The platform does not verify that the recorded dependencies are trusted. Non-hermetic builds can fetch arbitrary code during the build.

Level 4
- The level requires two-person review for all changes. The platform enforces hermetic builds. The provenance includes the complete build recipe and all resolved dependencies.
- The platform requires all inputs to be declared before the build. The build environment has no network access. A consumer verifies the signature and can replay the build if it is reproducible.
- Unaddressed threats: SLSA v1.0 does not require reproducible builds. Two consumers cannot automatically compare outputs. A compromised platform root or a malicious reviewer can still pass a bad change. Dependency vulnerabilities remain possible.

Edge cases
- Build dependencies: Levels 1 and 2 do not require a complete dependency list. Level 3 records dependencies but does not verify their trust. Level 4 requires hermetic resolution with immutable references for all dependencies.
- Hermeticity: Only Level 4 requires it. Without hermeticity, a build can pull a different dependency version on each run. The absence of hermeticity makes the provenance incomplete.
- Reproducible builds: SLSA v1.0 does not require reproducible builds. They are a separate property that enables independent verification. Level 4 does not guarantee identical outputs.

The population variance is a parameter. The sample variance is a statistic that estimates it.

Population variance:
σ² = (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^{N} (x_i − μ)²

Sample variance with Bessel's correction:
s² = (1/(n−1)) Σ_{i=1}^{n} (x_i − x̄)²

In these formulas, x_i denotes an observation. μ denotes the population mean. x̄ denotes the sample mean. N denotes the population size. n denotes the sample size.

When to use each:
- The population variance is appropriate when you measure every member of a finite population.
- The population variance is also appropriate when you know the exact distribution and its parameters.
- The sample variance is appropriate when you estimate a population variance from a random sample.
- Bessel's correction uses n−1 because the sample mean consumes one degree of freedom.

Unbiasedness:
For independent and identically distributed observations with finite variance, s² is an unbiased estimator of σ². The correction does not make s an unbiased estimator of σ. This result does not require a normal distribution. If you divide by n instead of n−1, the expected value is (n−1)/n times σ². That estimator is biased downward.

Effect on confidence intervals and hypothesis tests:
For a normal population with unknown variance, the confidence interval for the mean uses s and the t distribution:
x̄ ± t_{n−1, 1−α/2} · s/√n

The t distribution accounts for the extra uncertainty from the estimated variance. A test of a mean uses the statistic:
t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n)

When the population variance is known and the data are normal, the z interval uses σ:
x̄ ± z_{1−α/2} · σ/√n

If you use n in the denominator instead of n−1, the variance estimate is too small on average. Then standard errors are too small. Then confidence intervals are too narrow. Then tests reject the null too often. The type I error rate exceeds the nominal level.

For a test of a population variance with normal data, the statistic is:
χ² = ((n−1)s²)/σ₀²

This statistic has a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom. If you divide by n in s², this statistic has the wrong distribution unless you scale it by n/(n−1).

Assumptions about the data distribution:
- Independent observations.
- Identically distributed observations.
- Finite variance.
- Exact t intervals for a mean and chi-square tests for a variance require a normal population.
- Large-sample intervals for the mean are approximately valid without normal data, but the variance must be finite.

In northwestern Europe from about 1500 to 1800, cities gained more legal and political autonomy than cities in the Yangtze Delta. Merchant-controlled city councils, charters, and urban courts enforced contracts and protected property. These institutions supported long-distance trade, bills of exchange, and joint-stock companies. In the Yangtze Delta, the imperial state appointed magistrates to run cities. Merchant guilds and native banks existed, but they lacked the corporate legal powers of European cities. The state and local gentry controlled key commercial rules and tax collection.

For infrastructure, northwestern Europe built canals, turnpike roads, and improved harbors through private toll companies and municipal debt. Dense water transport in the Low Countries and England cut the cost of transport for bulk goods. The Yangtze Delta already had a dense river and canal network. The Grand Canal and coastal shipping moved grain, cloth, and other goods. The state funded major waterworks for grain tribute and flood control. Local gentry and communities maintained dikes and polders. This system moved goods efficiently but served administrative and fiscal goals more than autonomous urban capital formation.

Thus the key difference was institutional. European cities created self-governing commercial bodies. Yangtze Delta cities remained administrative units in a unified empire. Both regions invested in water transport. Urban and merchant interests often built and financed European infrastructure. The state and rural gentry built and financed Chinese infrastructure.

## Numerical stability

The two-pass formula first computes the arithmetic mean. It then sums the squared deviations from that mean. This two-pass process is numerically stable when you use a compensated summation for the mean, such as Kahan summation. The second pass removes the mean offset from each value. The formula uses the sum of squared deviations divided by n minus 1. It is not an online algorithm.

Welford's algorithm computes the mean and the corrected sum of squares in one pass. It updates a count, a current mean, and a corrected sum of squares. It is numerically stable for broad stream data. Its relative error can exceed the two-pass error for data with a large constant offset and small variance. In typical stream analytics data, the difference is small. Both formulas divide by n minus 1 to get the sample variance.

For data with a large constant offset, subtract a baseline constant before either algorithm runs. This subtraction reduces rounding error from large offsets. It does not remove error already present in rounded input values.

## Storage and compute

- The two-pass formula needs O(n) memory or a replayable source. It needs two passes over all data.
- Welford's algorithm needs O(1) memory and one pass. Each item has a constant number of updates.
- Welford gives a current estimate after each item. Two-pass gives the estimate after the final pass.
- Basic Welford is append-only. For time-windowed analytics, use a variant that supports removal of old items.

## Recommendation

For an unbounded online stream, use Welford. It is the standard choice for one-pass sample variance. For a finite stored batch where maximum accuracy is critical, use the two-pass formula. A hybrid approach is to run Welford on values shifted by a baseline and use extended precision for the mean and M2.

No, the assumption is false for the default behavior of typical pub-sub brokers. In typical pub-sub brokers, by default a message reaches only subscribers that are connected at the time of publication. A late subscriber does not receive that message by default. The broker does not store arbitrary messages for unknown future subscribers. The broker can store for a subscriber only if the broker knows the subscription. For example, a subscriber must create a JMS durable subscription before it goes offline.

Some systems provide features that store messages for later delivery. MQTT has a retained message feature. A broker stores only the last retained message on a topic and sends it to new subscribers. JMS durable subscriptions let a broker store messages while a known durable subscriber is offline. Log-based systems such as Apache Kafka store messages for a retention period. A new consumer can read old messages from the log if the consumer starts from the earliest offset and the messages remain within retention limits.

These features require explicit configuration or a retained message flag. If a publisher sends a message before any subscriber exists, the message does not reach later subscribers in the default configuration of typical pub-sub brokers. Individual broker documentation gives the exact behavior.

To proofread a document means to find and correct surface errors. These errors include misspelled words, punctuation, capitalization, and format errors. To edit a document means to check and change the content, structure, and clarity. To proofread and to edit are different tasks. They involve different types of review.

A proofread pass focuses on three surface error groups.
- It checks for typos, wrong homophones, and incorrect capitalization.
- It checks for omitted or extra punctuation marks.
- It checks for format errors, for example, heading styles, font sizes, and margins.
A separate pass for each error group reduces missed errors.

Formal document workflows separate the proofread pass from the content edit pass. A content edit changes words and sentences. New errors can appear after a content edit. If you proofread during a content edit, you can miss surface errors. A separate pass lets you focus on surface errors only. The proofread pass starts after all content edits are complete.

Content-type selection guidelines

application/json is suitable when:
- The payload represents data objects, arrays, numbers, strings, or booleans.
- The client or server works with JavaScript.
- The API must minimize message size and parse time.
- The consumer does not require XML namespaces, attributes, or mixed content.

application/xml is suitable when:
- The payload requires XML namespaces, attributes, or mixed content.
- The API contract or an existing system requires XML.
- Standard schema validation is a requirement.
- The payload is document-centric or follows an XML-based standard.

multipart/form-data is suitable only for request bodies when:
- The request includes one or more files.
- The request combines text fields and binary data.
- The client follows the HTML form submission rules.

For response bodies:
- application/json is suitable for most response bodies.
- application/xml is suitable when the response contract requires XML.
- multipart/form-data is not suitable for response bodies.
- If a response must contain multiple parts, the media types multipart/mixed and multipart/related are suitable.

Key trade-offs

application/json:
- It is smaller than application/xml for many data structures.
- It parses faster in JavaScript environments.
- It does not support namespaces, attributes, or mixed content.
- It does not include a built-in schema validation mechanism.

application/xml:
- It supports namespaces, attributes, mixed content, and standard schema validation.
- It is larger and parses slower than equivalent JSON.
- It matches many document-centric and enterprise systems.

multipart/form-data:
- It handles binary file uploads and mixed text and binary content.
- It adds boundary and part headers to each message.
- It does not provide nested data structures.
- It is not suitable for response bodies.

The Authorization request header carries credentials from a client to a server. The header value has this format: the scheme name, a space, and the credential. The server uses the scheme name to select the handler for the credential. This document explains three common schemes: Bearer tokens, Basic authentication, and API keys.

Bearer tokens use the format 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. The token can be an opaque string or a JSON Web Token. The server verifies the token with a signature check, a token store lookup, or both. Bearer token authentication does not require the client to sign the request with a separate key. Any party that holds the token can use it. The service must protect Bearer tokens with TLS.

Basic authentication uses the format 'Authorization: Basic <base64(username:password)>'. The client encodes the username and password with Base64. Base64 is a reversible code. The server decodes the header and checks the password. Basic authentication is simple for small services, but it sends the full credentials on each request. The server must use TLS to protect the credentials.

API keys do not have a standard Authorization scheme. For example, a service can use 'Authorization: ApiKey <key>' or a custom header like 'X-API-Key'. The key identifies an application or a project, not always a user. An API key is often a long random string. The service stores the key and checks it on each request. An API key is simpler to issue and revoke than user credentials, but a leaked key gives broad access.

Possible reasons that npm ignores or updates the lockfile:

- The CI job uses `npm install` and not `npm ci`. The `npm install` command can update package-lock.json and can install newer patch releases that match the semver ranges in package.json.
- The package.json file and package-lock.json are out of sync. If a dependency or script changed in package.json, `npm install` re-resolves the tree and updates the lockfile.
- package-lock.json is not present in the build. The file can be missing from the repository, excluded by .gitignore, or not committed in the CI branch.
- The npm version in CI differs from the local version. A newer npm version can migrate the lockfile and change resolved versions.
- A setting disables package locks, such as `package-lock=false` in .npmrc or `npm_config_package_lock=false`. npm does not read or write the lockfile.
- A build step runs `npm update` or installs a package manually. That step can refresh transitive dependencies and write a new lockfile.

Steps to confirm whether the lockfile was used:

1. Open the CI build log. Find the command that installs dependencies. Confirm that the command is `npm ci` and not `npm install`.
2. Confirm that package-lock.json is in the build workspace. Run `git status --short package-lock.json` before the install step. The file must be listed.
3. Compare the lockfile in the build with the committed version. Run `git diff --exit-code HEAD -- package-lock.json` before the install step. The command must produce no output.
4. Inspect npm configuration. Run `npm config get package-lock` in the CI job. The output must be `true`.
5. Confirm the npm version in CI. Run `npm --version`. Compare this version with the `lockfileVersion` field in package-lock.json.
6. Run `npm ci` on a clean local copy with the committed lockfile. Confirm that the transitive package installs at the locked version. Run `npm ls <transitive-package>` to see the installed version.
7. If `npm ci` fails with a lockfile mismatch, update package-lock.json from package.json. Then run the build again.
8. If the version still changes, run `npm explain <transitive-package>` to see the resolution chain.

Triage of incoming bug reports separates urgent defects from minor issues. It assigns each report to a category and an owner. It prevents team overload and keeps critical bugs visible.

First, a triage member verifies the report. The member verifies that the bug exists and that the details are complete, then reproduces the bug in a test environment. The member assesses severity and frequency. The member records the impact and the number of users or events that the bug affects. The member estimates required developer time with a relative value, for example small, medium, or large. The member assigns a priority and an owner, links the report to a release or a backlog item, and records the decision and the reason.

A priority matrix compares severity, frequency, and required effort. Severity measures the impact when the bug occurs. Frequency measures how often the bug occurs or how many users it affects, and developer time measures the effort to fix the bug. High severity and high frequency with low effort get the highest priority. When effort is high, the team can split the fix or plan it for a later release. Low severity and rare bugs wait.

A CvRDT and a CmRDT converge by different rules. Both approaches can guarantee eventual convergence when their required conditions are met.

A CvRDT replica sends its current state to other replicas. The receiver merges the received state into its local state. The merge operation must be associative, commutative, and idempotent. Convergence follows from these merge properties. This approach tolerates lost, duplicated, or reordered messages. Any later message that carries an equal or newer state repairs the missing update.

A CmRDT replica sends each update operation to other replicas. The replicas that receive the message apply each operation to their local state. The operations must commute. The dissemination layer must deliver every operation to every replica. Common implementations use reliable causal broadcast. The operation messages are small when the state is large.

Operation-based CmRDT is preferable in these edge cases:
- The state is large and each update changes only a small part. A full-state CvRDT can send the entire state after every update.
- The update rate is high and bandwidth is limited. Operation messages are much smaller than full states.
- The update operations have a clean commutative formulation. The merge function for the full state is difficult to write or compute.

State-based CvRDT is preferable in these edge cases:
- The network drops, duplicates, or reorders messages. CvRDT does not need exactly-once delivery.
- Replicas stay disconnected for long periods. A later merge of full states repairs all missing updates.
- A new replica joins the system. It can copy one current state. It does not have to replay an operation log.
- The full state is small and the merge function is cheap. CvRDT is simpler because it needs no special message layer.

CORS is a browser mechanism that controls cross-origin HTTP requests. The browser applies different rules for simple requests, preflighted requests, and credentialed requests. The following descriptions follow the Fetch standard. Implementations can vary by browser version.

Simple requests

A simple cross-origin request uses only GET, HEAD, or POST. It uses only CORS-safelisted request headers. If POST has a body, its content type must be one of these three values: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain. The browser sends the actual request immediately with an Origin header.

To permit the response, the server must include the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. Its value can be the exact origin or an asterisk. If the header is absent or does not match, the browser blocks the response from the script. If the response has custom response headers, the server must also include Access-Control-Expose-Headers so the script can read them.

Preflighted requests

A request is not simple when it uses a method other than GET, HEAD, or POST. It is also not simple when it includes a custom header such as Authorization or X-API-Key. It is not simple when the POST body uses a content type other than the three safe values, for example application/json.

The browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight request to the same URL for such requests. The preflight request includes these headers: Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, and Access-Control-Request-Headers. To permit the request, the server must respond to the preflight with Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

The response must include Access-Control-Allow-Methods with all allowed methods for the resource. The response must include Access-Control-Allow-Headers with all allowed request headers. The server can also include Access-Control-Max-Age to cache the preflight response for a number of seconds. If the preflight response does not grant permission, the browser blocks the actual request. If the preflight succeeds, the browser sends the actual request. The actual response must include Access-Control-Allow-Origin with a value that matches the origin.

Credentialed requests

A credentialed cross-origin request includes cookies, HTTP authentication entries, or client TLS certificates. JavaScript enables credentials by setting withCredentials to true on XMLHttpRequest or by setting credentials to include on fetch. The browser does not send credentials by default on cross-origin requests.

To permit a credentialed response, the server must set Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact origin. It must not use the asterisk value. The server must also include Access-Control-Allow-Credentials with value true. If either header is missing or wrong, the browser blocks the response.

For a preflighted credentialed request, the preflight response must include the same two headers. The preflight response must not use an asterisk for Access-Control-Allow-Methods or Access-Control-Allow-Headers. It must list the actual methods and headers.

This comparison describes common implementations. Exact results depend on the project.

Dependency management: In a layered architecture, each layer depends on the layer below it. In some implementations, this direction permits infrastructure details to enter the domain layer. Hexagonal architecture separates the domain from external systems with ports and adapters. The domain depends only on ports. Adapters depend on the domain.

Testability: In a layered architecture, tests often use mocks for lower layers. The domain code can still depend on framework objects. Hexagonal architecture lets developers test the domain with fake adapters. Separate integration tests cover the real adapters.

Cost of new external integrations: In a layered architecture, a new integration often requires changes in lower layers and in the layer above them. Hexagonal architecture has lower cost if a port already exists. You write one new adapter and connect it to the domain. If no port exists, you must add a port and update all implementations.

There are two main types of borders.

People, not land, usually create straight borders. Governments or treaty makers drew these lines with latitude, longitude, or survey lines. They often did not know or did not use local geography. For example, the western part of the border between the United States and Canada follows the 49th parallel. Many borders in Africa from the colonial era are also straight.

Borders that follow rivers or mountains are natural boundaries. A river or a mountain ridge is a clear physical barrier. It separates people, trade, and movement. These features are easy to identify on maps and on the ground. For example, the Rio Grande forms part of the border between the United States and Mexico. The Pyrenees form much of the border between France and Spain.

Some straight borders ignore local communities and resources. They can split ethnic groups or water sources. Natural borders can change when a river moves its course, and this causes disputes. The shape of a border shows its history. Straight lines often show a treaty made far away. Curved lines often show a border that grew from the land.

## Steps to build and maintain motivation

1. Define one specific long-term academic goal.
2. Break that goal into weekly tasks.
3. Schedule each task as a fixed block in a calendar.
4. Start each study block with a 2-minute task to lower friction.
5. Track completed tasks with a visible checklist.
6. Review the checklist at the end of each day.
7. Connect each task to the long-term goal before you start.
8. If motivation drops, reduce the task to a 5-minute version.
9. After one week, evaluate which schedule times worked.
10. Adjust the schedule but keep the fixed start time.
11. Use a reward only after a completed task, not before.
12. Share your weekly goal with one study partner.
13. Repeat steps 3 through 12 each week.

## Trade-offs to watch

- Fixed schedules increase consistency. They reduce flexibility for unexpected events.
- Public commitment increases accountability. It also adds social pressure.
- Rewards improve short-term compliance. They can weaken intrinsic interest over time.
- A fixed routine reduces decision fatigue. It can cause boredom.
- Short tasks lower entry friction. They can encourage shallow work.
- Daily review increases awareness. It increases time cost.
- Frequent adjustments reduce boredom. They break habit formation.

Git tags are not truly immutable. They are refs, similar to branches, that point to a commit or to a tag object. A branch advances automatically when you commit on that branch. A tag does not advance automatically. Git does not enforce immutability. You can move a tag with a forced command.

Locally, the command `git tag <name> <commit>` fails if a tag with that name already exists and points to a different object. To move the tag, you must use `git tag --force <name> <commit>`. The short form is `git tag -f <name> <commit>`. This updates the local ref to the new target. The previous tag target remains in the object database until garbage collection removes it.

On a remote, `git push origin <tag>` fails if the remote already has that tag with a different target. To overwrite the remote tag, you must use `git push --force origin <tag>`. Other clones keep the old tag until they fetch with the force option or delete and fetch the tag again.

Standard Git alone does not enforce tag immutability. Hosting services such as GitHub or GitLab can add tag protection rules. Those rules are outside the scope of core Git.

# Git Merge and Git Rebase Reference

This document describes two Git commands that combine changes from one branch into another.
The commands are `git merge` and `git rebase`.
The examples use a local repository with a `main` branch and a `feature` branch.

## What `git merge` does

`git merge` integrates changes from a source branch into the current branch.
The command creates a new merge commit on the current branch.
The merge commit has two parents: the previous tip of the current branch and the tip of the source branch.
The original commits from both branches stay in the history.
The history shows a fork and a join point.

Example:
You are on the `main` branch and run `git merge feature`.
Git creates a merge commit that contains the changes from the `feature` branch.
The `main` branch now includes the `feature` changes.

## What `git rebase` does

`git rebase` moves or replays the commits of the current branch onto the tip of another branch.
The command creates new commits with new hashes for each moved commit.
The original commits are no longer reachable from the branch.
The new history is linear.
A rebase rewrites the branch history.

Example:
You are on the `feature` branch and run `git rebase main`.
Git takes the commits that are unique to `feature` and replays them on top of `main`.
The `feature` branch now has a linear history.

## When to use merge

A merge is suitable when any of these conditions is true:
- You want to preserve the exact history of both branches.
- You work on a shared branch that other people use.
- You want a merge commit that records the integration.
- You integrate a long-lived branch, such as a release branch.

## When to use rebase

A rebase is suitable when all of these conditions are true:
- You want a clean, linear history.
- You work on a local feature branch that no other person uses.
- You want to update the feature branch with the latest changes from `main`.
- You can force-push the branch after the rebase, if the branch is on a remote.

## Important conditions

`git rebase` changes commit hashes.
If you pushed the branch to a remote, you must force-push after the rebase.
Force-push is safe only on a branch that you own.
If a rebase conflict occurs, Git stops the rebase.
A conflict requires you to resolve it and then run `git rebase --continue`.

Technical documentation is a set of written materials. It describes a product, a system, or a process. It explains how the product works and how to use it. It helps readers complete tasks and solve problems. It serves customers, operators, and developers.

Technical documentation can be procedural or descriptive. Procedural text tells readers what to do. Descriptive text explains how a product works. A document can contain both types. A writer keeps the two types separate in each section.

Common forms

Technical documentation has many forms. The form depends on the audience and the product.

- A user guide explains how to operate the product.
- An API reference lists the functions, parameters, and return values.
- A runbook gives procedures for common operational tasks.
- Release notes describe the changes in a software version.
- An installation guide explains how to set up the product.
- A fault diagnosis guide helps readers find and fix problems.
- An architecture document describes the components of a system and their connections.
- A frequently asked questions page answers common questions.

What an effective document must include

An effective document must include these elements.

- A title that states the subject.
- A statement that identifies the audience.
- A scope section that lists the topics the document covers.
- A list of prerequisites for procedures.
- Step-by-step procedures with one action per step.
- Expected results for each step.
- Error recovery actions.
- A glossary that defines new terms.
- Examples that show real input and output.
- Version information and a date.
- Links to related documents.

This guidance describes a reusable template for technical reports. A reusable template has four parts: metadata, summary, body, and appendix. The metadata block identifies the report. The summary communicates key findings. The body provides evidence and analysis. The appendix stores reference material.

Required fields

The template defines variables for these fields:
- Title
- Author or owner
- Date
- Version
- Status (draft, review, approved)
- Audience or distribution list
- Purpose
- Scope
- Key findings
- Body sections
- Conclusion
- References

The template must not contain hardcoded values. Hardcoded values cause errors when authors reuse the template.

Trade-offs

Flexibility lets authors adjust the template for different report types. Consistency helps readers find information quickly and compare reports. Too much flexibility creates unstructured reports. Too much consistency prevents necessary detail.

Recommendation

A balanced template has fixed required sections and one blank custom section. Each required section has a title, a heading level, and a maximum length. Project teams review the template after every three uses. They change only the custom section. This practice gives a balance between flexibility and consistency.

Consistent hashing is a method to assign data items to a set of storage nodes. It uses a hash ring. The ring is a circular order of hash output values.

A hash function maps each node identifier and each data key to a position on this ring. A key belongs to the first node that appears clockwise from the key position. If no node appears clockwise, the key belongs to the first node on the ring. This rule gives a stable assignment for a fixed node set.

When a node joins, only keys that now map to the new node move. When a node leaves, only keys that mapped to that node move to the next clockwise node. Other keys keep their assignment. This property limits data movement.

With few nodes, the positions on the ring can be uneven. One node can own a large arc and receive many more keys than another node. This is load skew.

Virtual nodes reduce this skew. Each physical node is represented by many points on the ring. Each point has a different hash input. A key maps to a virtual node, and the virtual node maps to its physical node. More virtual nodes make the ownership arcs more even on average. Virtual nodes do not eliminate skew from hot keys or from a poor hash function.

Under a node failure, the system must detect the failure and remove the failed node from the ring. The failed node's virtual nodes disappear, and keys that mapped to them now map to the next clockwise virtual node. Until detection, requests to the failed node can fail. After removal, no key data is lost if replicas exist elsewhere. Consistent hashing only assigns responsibility. It does not provide replication or durability.

Under a node addition, the system inserts the new node's virtual nodes. The new node takes ownership of keys between each new virtual node and the previous clockwise node. The previous owners release those keys. The number of moved keys is usually proportional to the number of added virtual nodes divided by the total number of virtual nodes.

If all nodes fail or the ring is empty, no node exists for any key. The system must handle this condition explicitly. If a hash maps two nodes or two keys to the same position, the system must define a collision rule. If key distribution is highly skewed, consistent hashing does not balance it. Application-level partitioning or key redesign is necessary. Weighted virtual nodes can give more ring positions to nodes with more capacity, but this is a policy choice.

Check these items first:

1. Check that the query text and the indexed text use the same preprocessing.
2. If the embedding model requires a query prefix, check that the prefix is present.
3. Check the document chunk size and overlap because chunks that are too small lose context.
4. Check that the embedding model fits the domain of the documents.
5. Check the similarity metric. If the vectors are not normalized, use cosine similarity.
6. Check that the index vectors were generated by the current embedding model.

A wave moves energy through a medium or space. Wave speed is the distance a wave travels in one second. Frequency is the number of cycles per second. Wavelength is the distance between two identical points on adjacent cycles. For a single-frequency wave, the speed equals the frequency multiplied by the wavelength. All values must use the same unit system.

Procedure
1. Identify the frequency value.
2. Identify the wavelength value.
3. If the frequency unit is not hertz, convert it to hertz.
4. If the wavelength unit is not meters, convert it to meters.
5. Multiply the frequency in hertz by the wavelength in meters.
6. Write the product with the unit meters per second (m/s).

Example
For a wave with frequency 5 hertz and wavelength 2 meters, the speed is 10 meters per second.

1. Record process resident set size and committed heap size at fixed intervals for a fixed duration.
2. If memory growth continues without a plateau, proceed.
3. Before you use a profiler, do not run it against production traffic. Profilers add overhead and change timing.
4. Install a heap profiler that supports your allocator.
5. Capture a heap snapshot at the start of a controlled workload.
6. Run the workload for a fixed period.
7. Capture a second heap snapshot at the end.
8. Compare allocated bytes and allocation stacks between the two snapshots.
9. If the same stacks allocate memory without a matching free, inspect those code sites. Verify that the code eventually frees all allocated blocks.
10. Measure live object size in both snapshots with a live heap analysis.
11. If live object size and allocated bytes are stable, examine fragmentation and allocator retention.
12. If live object size increases, inspect the object graph from static roots. Look for global collections, caches, listener registrations, and thread-local objects.
13. For fragmentation, reduce many small allocations. Use a pool allocator or larger contiguous allocations.
14. Check allocator statistics and per-thread caches. If cache bytes grow while requested bytes remain stable, call the allocator trim function after low activity. Short-lived threads can retain memory in per-thread caches. Use a thread pool for short-lived threads. Clear thread-local objects before thread exit.
15. After a fix, repeat the same workload. Compare the memory slope. Run a long-duration test. Watch for reintroduction.

In CPython, reference counting is the primary mechanism for object lifetime. Each new reference increases the reference count by one. Each removed reference decreases the count by one. When the count reaches zero, CPython deallocates the object immediately. This release is deterministic. It does not wait for a separate collection cycle.

Reference counting cannot free cycles by itself. A cycle occurs when two or more objects refer to each other. Their counts never reach zero. CPython includes a cyclic tracing collector. This collector finds and frees unreachable cycles. It runs periodically or when a threshold is crossed.

Tracing collectors scan all reachable objects from roots. They free unreachable objects in one pass. Tracing adds less overhead to each pointer operation. But it can pause the program during collection, while reference counting spreads overhead across assignments and releases. It can release memory sooner. It cannot handle cycles without a supplementary collector.

Weak references do not increase the reference count. You can create them with the weakref module. An object that has only weak references is deallocated. Weak references suit caches and observer lists. They help prevent leaks from long-lived containers. They do not break cycles by themselves.

Rate limiting protects the API from overload. It can also block some legitimate requests. This trade-off affects user experience.

Algorithms differ in accuracy and memory use. A fixed window resets counts at fixed intervals. It can allow two bursts at window boundaries. A token bucket permits bursts up to the bucket size. It refills at a steady rate. A sliding window log is accurate but uses more memory.

A sliding window counter is less accurate than a sliding window log. It uses less memory. The required accuracy and memory limits determine the algorithm choice.

Follow these steps to add rate limiting:
1. Verify that authentication returns a stable user identifier.
2. Choose the enforcement point: API gateway if available, otherwise application middleware.
3. Select one rate limiting algorithm.
4. Set separate limits for each endpoint category. Use higher limits for read endpoints and lower limits for write endpoints.
5. Use a fast data store that supports atomic increment and expiry.
6. Implement the limiter at the chosen point.
7. Add these headers to each response:
   - X-RateLimit-Limit
   - X-RateLimit-Remaining
   - X-RateLimit-Reset
8. Return HTTP 429 for requests above the limit. Include a Retry-After header in the 429 response.
9. Write a clear error message for the 429 response. Tell the user when to retry.
10. Do not apply rate limits to health checks or authentication endpoints. A strict limit can lock out users.
11. Test with requests at the limit and above the limit. Confirm that requests above the limit return HTTP 429.
12. Monitor error rates and user complaints after deployment. If the error rate is high, adjust the limits.
13. Keep the previous configuration for rollback. If the new limits cause failures, restore the previous configuration.

A daily walk-around check is a quick external check that a driver performs. A formal safety inspection is a detailed technical inspection that a qualified technician performs. The daily check and the formal safety inspection do not replace each other.

## What Each Includes

**Daily walk-around check**
The walk-around check covers these items:
- tires and wheels
- lights and reflectors
- mirrors and windshield
- brakes and air lines
- fluids and leaks
- coupling devices
- cargo securement

The daily check gives a quick external view of the vehicle.

**Formal safety inspection**
The inspection covers these items:
- brake condition and adjustment
- steering and suspension components
- exhaust and fuel systems
- wheels, rims, and tires
- emergency equipment
- frame and body condition

The technician measures wear and checks for leaks, corrosion, and hidden damage.
Some formal inspections also include a road test.

## How Often

A driver must perform the daily walk-around check before the first trip of each day.
Some fleets require another check after a long stop or a driver change.

A formal safety inspection must occur at the interval set by law or by the fleet maintenance program.
In many regulatory systems, this interval is at least once per year.
A truck that operates in severe conditions can require formal inspections more often.

## Consequences If Skipped

If a driver skips the daily check, a defect can stay hidden until the vehicle moves.
That defect can cause a breakdown, a crash, or a citation at a roadside check.
The driver and the carrier can also face liability if the defect adds to an incident.

If a carrier or owner skips the formal safety inspection, wear and hidden damage can become severe before anyone finds them.
The carrier can face penalties for the absence of a valid inspection record.
A missed inspection also increases the chance of a sudden failure that causes a crash.

# Home Insulation Guide

## How Insulation Works

Heat moves from warm areas to cold areas.
Insulation slows this heat flow.
The R-value measures resistance to heat flow.
A higher R-value gives more insulation.
The best R-value for your home depends on your climate and local building codes.

## Main Insulation Materials

The three common materials have different properties.

- Fiberglass is made from fine glass fibers. It comes in batts, rolls, and loose fill. Fibers can irritate skin and lungs during installation. Protective clothing and a respirator are necessary.
- Foam insulation includes spray foam and rigid foam boards. Spray foam expands to fill cavities and seal air leaks. Rigid foam gives a high R-value per inch of thickness.
- Cellulose is made from recycled paper with fire retardant. Installers blow it into cavities with special equipment. Cellulose can settle over time and lose some R-value.

## Factors by Area

### Attic

The attic is the most important area for insulation because heat rises.
Loose fill or batts go between the ceiling joists.
The soffit vents must remain clear of insulation.
Blocked vents prevent air flow and cause moisture problems.
The required attic R-value is higher than the wall R-value in most climates.

### Walls

For new construction, batts or spray foam fit inside the wall cavities.
For existing walls, a contractor can inject dense-pack cellulose or foam through small holes.
The insulation must fill each cavity completely without gaps.

### Basements and Crawl Spaces

Rigid foam boards insulate foundation walls in basements.
In crawl spaces, insulation goes on the walls or on the floor above.
The correct choice depends on whether the crawl space is ventilated or sealed.

## Moisture Control and Ventilation

Air leaks carry moisture into wall and attic cavities.
All air leaks must be sealed before insulation is added.
Caulk and foam sealant close gaps around pipes, wires, and electrical boxes.
Moisture that condenses in insulation reduces the R-value and can cause mold.

Vapor barriers slow moisture movement through walls.
In cold climates, the vapor barrier must be on the warm side of the wall.
In hot humid climates, a vapor barrier can trap moisture inside the wall.
A local building expert can give climate-specific advice.

Soffit vents and ridge vents work together so that air flows from the eaves to the peak.
Insulation must not cover the vents.
A balanced ventilation system prevents condensation on the roof deck.

## Planning and Safety

Local building codes set minimum R-values and installation rules.
These requirements must be confirmed before materials are purchased.
A professional energy audit can find air leaks and insulation gaps.
Some insulation types require special equipment and protective gear.
You can install fiberglass batts yourself, but spray foam and blown cellulose often require a contractor.

Insulation must not be installed over damaged wiring.
An electrician must inspect damaged wiring before insulation work begins.
Insulation must remain away from recessed light fixtures unless the fixture is rated for insulation contact.

## Properties of common wait time distributions

Wait times are positive continuous values. They often have a long right tail. Two common distributions are the exponential and the lognormal. If neither distribution fits, consider the gamma distribution or the Weibull distribution.

- Exponential distribution: one parameter. It models the time between independent events that occur at a constant rate. The density is highest at zero and decreases. The hazard rate is constant.

- Lognormal distribution: two parameters. The natural log of the data follows a normal distribution. The density is zero at zero, rises to a peak, and then decreases. The hazard rate first increases and then decreases.

## How to decide between them

A histogram supplies the first clue. If the density decreases from a maximum near zero, the exponential distribution is more plausible. If the density rises from zero to a peak and then declines, the lognormal distribution is more plausible. This rule is not a formal test. It can fail with small samples.

## Procedure to check the fit

Use these steps.

1. Load the wait time data into a statistical tool.
2. Plot a histogram of the data.
3. Plot a quantile-quantile plot for the exponential distribution.
4. Plot a quantile-quantile plot for the lognormal distribution.
5. Fit the exponential distribution to the data.
6. Fit the lognormal distribution to the data.
7. Record the Akaike information criterion value for each fit.
8. Compare the two quantile-quantile plots.
9. Choose the distribution with points closer to a straight line.
10. Compare the two Akaike information criterion values.
11. Choose the distribution with the smaller value.

## Interpretation

A quantile-quantile plot shows the observed quantiles against the theoretical quantiles. A good fit places the points near the reference line. The Akaike information criterion measures relative fit. A smaller value means better fit after a penalty for extra parameters. No test proves that a distribution is the true data-generating process. The result is evidence from a sample.

HTTP status codes tell the client if the request succeeded or failed. A status code is a three-digit number in the response.

4xx codes mean a client error. Common codes include 400 for a bad request and 404 for a missing resource. 5xx codes mean a server error. Common codes include 500 for an internal server error and 503 for a service that is not available.

Many APIs include an error body. This body often contains fields such as code, message, and details. The code field is a machine-readable identifier for the error type. The message field is a short human-readable description. The details field can contain extra information about invalid parameters. Not all APIs use the same field names or format.

Consistent error formats matter for client code. If the format is consistent, the client can parse the error code from one location. The client can then decide how to handle the error. For example, it can retry on a 429 or 503 status. The client can show the message field to a user. The client can log the code and details to debug the problem.

If the format changes between endpoints, the client needs a separate parser for each endpoint. This requirement increases code complexity and bugs. The API documentation defines the exact error format for that API.

Traditional plus/minus tolerancing gives each linear dimension a permitted range. For example, a hole diameter can be 10.00 mm plus or minus 0.05 mm. The drawing shows sizes and distances from edges. It controls the size and the position of each feature. It does not state how round or straight a surface must be. It can be ambiguous when many dimensions chain from one edge to another.

Geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T) uses symbols and feature control frames. It states the allowed deviation for form, orientation, location, and runout. A datum is a reference surface or axis that the tolerance relates to. GD&T can specify a cylindrical tolerance zone for a hole position. It can control size, form, and location with separate symbols. These controls are defined in standards such as ASME Y14.5.

A manufacturer chooses plus/minus tolerancing for simple parts that do not mate with other parts. This method is easy to read and often costs less to inspect. A manufacturer chooses GD&T when features must align or fit at assembly, when form is critical, or when many features share one reference. GD&T requires more study, but it gives a clearer functional definition. The choice depends on the part function and the available inspection equipment.
